title: Google Drive (Cloud File Storage)
problem: Design a cloud file storage and sync service like Google Drive, Dropbox, or OneDrive.
summary: A sync-centric file-storage service built around content-addressed block storage. Per the book's final design, the upload path fans into three asynchronous flows: (1) the block server splits the file into 4 MB blocks, compresses + encrypts them, and uploads only the blocks whose SHA-256 hash isn't already present (delta sync + dedup); (2) the metadata service writes the new file row / chunk manifest to the metadata DB (with a Redis metadata cache in front of it); (3) the notification service pushes the change to every other device the user is signed into so sync happens in seconds. Storage is optimized by (a) block-level deduplication across users, (b) a cold-storage / offline-backup tier for old versions and rarely-accessed blocks, and (c) version-history limits (keep N recent versions, or time-based retention) so a single user's 100 rewrites of the same doc don't blow up storage forever.

functional: Upload, download, rename, move, and delete files and folders
Version history: fetch and restore any previous revision
Multi-device sync within seconds of a commit
Delta / changes-since-revision API for sync clients
Sharing with per-user or per-link ACLs and collaborative edits
Full-text and filename search across the user's corpus
Offline edits that reconcile on reconnect
nonFunctional: 99.99% availability for metadata reads and writes
P99 sync notification delivery under 1 second
Block-level dedup yielding at least 30% storage savings
Scale to 100M DAU, 3 devices per user, 1 PB/day ingress
Strong read-after-write consistency inside a single user's namespace

assumptions: 100M DAU, 10 file operations/user/day → 1B ops/day, ~70% reads / 30% writes
Average file 1 MB, P99 file 1 GB; block size = 4 MB (fixed)
50B files lifetime, ~10 PB raw, but dedup ratio ~30% → ~7 PB physical after dedup
Version history retention: last 10 versions OR 30 days, whichever is smaller — older versions drop to cold storage
Cross-device sync: avg 3 devices per active user — notification service fans out on every commit
Collaborative edits: ~1% of files shared, avg 3 collaborators
Search index over filename + OCR'd content for ~5B files
estimates: Upload bandwidth: 1 PB/day / 86400 ≈ 12 GB/s aggregate across regions
Metadata DB size: 50B files * ~500B row + 50B * 250 blocks * 80B chunk ref ≈ 25 TB files + 1 PB block manifests → shard across ~100 SQL nodes
Redis cache: hottest 10M files' metadata ≈ 50 GB — fits a small Redis cluster
Notification connections: 100M DAU * 3 devices * 30% online = 90M active long-poll / WS connections

client.name: Client (Desktop Sync / Web / Mobile)
client.summary: Desktop sync agent, web app, or mobile app that chunks files locally, runs delta sync, and holds a long-lived connection to the notification service for multi-device updates.

sections.heading: Local chunking + SHA-256
sections.body: Client splits each file into fixed 4 MB blocks. For each block it computes a SHA-256 hash (the book's block hash). The hash is both the dedup key and the integrity check — the server re-verifies on receipt.

sections.heading: Delta sync
sections.body: When a file changes, the client re-chunks it, diffs the new block-hash list against the previous revision, and sends ONLY the changed block hashes to the block servers. A 1 GB video edited in one place → maybe 1 new 4 MB block uploaded instead of the whole gigabyte. This is the dominant bandwidth savings for collaborative documents.

sections.heading: Resumable upload
sections.body: Each block upload is a separate PUT; failures resume per-block, not per-file. A 1 GB file is 250 blocks — one transient network blip kills one block, not the entire upload.

sections.heading: Notification / multi-device sync
sections.body: Every signed-in device holds a long-poll HTTP connection (or WebSocket) to the notification service. When Device A commits an edit, the notification service pushes the delta to Devices B and C within ~1s. They pull the changed-block list and re-download just those blocks — the book's picture of 'Drive sync felt instant'.

sections.heading: Why this matters for beginners
sections.body: Block-level dedup + delta sync + per-block resumable upload are what make 'upload my 50 GB photo library over hotel WiFi' actually work. Without them one lost packet ruins hours.

bottlenecks.title: Local SHA-256 hashing dominates large-file upload latency
bottlenecks.trigger: P99 file = 1 GB = 256 blocks of 4 MB; SHA-256 on commodity laptops runs ~400 MB/s single-threaded, so hashing a 1 GB file takes ~2.5s before a single byte leaves the machine. Worse on mobile/ARM (~150 MB/s → ~7s).
bottlenecks.symptom: User drags in a large file and the sync agent sits at 'Preparing…' for several seconds with no network activity; CPU pegged at 100% on one core; battery drain on laptops/phones.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Pipeline hashing with upload: hash block N while uploading block N-1 (producer/consumer with a 2–4 block buffer). Use hardware-accelerated SHA-NI (OpenSSL EVP) and parallelize across cores with a worker pool sized to min(ncpu, 4). On mobile, fall back to BLAKE3 for ~3x throughput where server accepts it.
bottlenecks.detection: Client telemetry histogram `client.prepare_ms` bucketed by file_size; alert when p95(prepare_ms)/p95(upload_ms) > 0.3 or when prepare_ms for >100MB files exceeds 1500ms.

bottlenecks.title: Long-poll/WebSocket connection churn on flaky networks
bottlenecks.trigger: Every signed-in device holds a persistent connection to the notification service (90M active at steady state). Mobile radio sleep, NAT rebinds (typical 5-min UDP / 30-min TCP timeout), captive portals, and laptop suspend/resume all break the connection, forcing reconnect + /changes?since=rev catch-up.
bottlenecks.symptom: Multi-device sync latency spikes from ~1s to tens of seconds after network transitions; 'file updated on other device' appears with noticeable delay after waking laptop or switching WiFi/LTE; duplicated change events seen after reconnect storms.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Exponential backoff with jitter (base 1s, cap 30s) on reconnect; resume via `since=rev` cursor rather than full resync; prefer WebSocket with ping/pong keepalive every 25s (under typical NAT timeout); on mobile, rely on FCM/APNs for wake-up instead of holding a socket in background; dedupe events client-side by (file_id, rev).
bottlenecks.detection: Track `client.notify.reconnect_rate` (target < 0.1/min/device) and `client.notify.catchup_lag_ms` p95 (alert > 5s); monitor `client.notify.duplicate_events_dropped` as a proxy for reconnect storms.

bottlenecks.title: Parallel block upload saturates a single user's uplink and head-of-lines other files
bottlenecks.trigger: A 1 GB file = 250 blocks. Naive fan-out (e.g., 16 concurrent PUTs) on a 10 Mbps home uplink drops per-connection throughput to ~80 KB/s each, and TCP fairness means any other app (Zoom, backup) shares the pipe badly. Also blocks other files queued behind it (head-of-line).
bottlenecks.symptom: User reports 'Drive is making my WiFi unusable' or 'small file I just dropped is stuck behind a big upload'; upload ETAs wildly inaccurate; Zoom calls degrade while sync is active.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Adaptive concurrency: start at 4 parallel PUTs, AIMD based on observed RTT/throughput (LEDBAC-style); separate queues for small (<10 MB) and large files so small files preempt; user-facing bandwidth cap setting (default: 75% of measured uplink); pause uploads when foreground latency-sensitive apps detected (OS hints on macOS/Windows).
bottlenecks.detection: Client metric `client.upload.goodput_bps` vs measured link capacity; alert when sustained goodput < 50% of link for >30s during an active upload; histogram `client.upload.small_file_queue_wait_ms` p95 > 5s indicates head-of-line blocking.

prebuild.explanation: ### Why the client is a real component here, not just "the browser" In most system designs, "client" is a thin box that makes HTTP requests. For Google Drive, the client is doing **serious work** — it chunks files into 4 MB blocks, computes SHA-256 hashes locally, diffs them against the previous revision, and only uploads what's new. This is not an optimization tacked on at the end; it's the foundation of the whole design. The server literally cannot do block-level dedup or delta sync unless the client has already split the file and hashed each piece before talking to the API. ### What goes wrong without a smart client If the client just POSTed whole files like a naive file upload form, then every time you tweaked one paragraph in a 1 GB video project, you'd re-upload the entire gigabyte. On hotel WiFi that's 15+ minutes per save. Worse, a single dropped packet near the end would restart the whole thing. The operator would see upload bandwidth usage explode, cloud storage costs balloon (no dedup possible server-side without knowing block boundaries), and support tickets flood in about "Drive ate my afternoon." ### The math at this scale The design estimates **12 GB/s aggregate upload bandwidth** and a **~30% dedup ratio**. That dedup ratio is only achievable because clients hash blocks before uploading — the server sees hashes and says "already have it, skip." If clients uploaded raw bytes and expected the server to dedup, the server would need to receive all 12 GB/s, hash it, *then* discard 3.6 GB/s as duplicates. Pushing that work to the client saves ~3.6 GB/s of wasted ingress bandwidth and the CPU to hash it server-side. ### The trade-off You accept that client code becomes complex and version-sensitive (every platform needs a correct, fast SHA-256 + chunking implementation) in exchange for making large-file sync actually usable over real-world networks.

lb.name: Load Balancer
lb.summary: L7 HTTPS load balancer fronting the API tier (metadata service + signed-URL issuance).

sections.heading: Scope
sections.body: API and metadata traffic flow through here. Actual block bytes go client → block servers → cloud storage — the LB never sees a 4 MB block payload.

sections.heading: Algorithm
sections.body: Round-robin across stateless API replicas; least-connections tie-break. Health check on /healthz.

sections.heading: TLS
sections.body: Terminates TLS at the edge; plaintext HTTP inside the VPC to the API tier.

lost: Control plane ops overhead

bottlenecks.title: TLS termination CPU saturates at peak API QPS
bottlenecks.trigger: Peak 35K QPS (10K write + 25K read) all terminate TLS at the LB. Mobile/desktop sync agents reconnect frequently (long-poll cycles, flaky networks across 90M active devices), causing full TLS handshakes rather than session resumption — each handshake costs ~1–3ms of CPU on a modern core.
bottlenecks.symptom: LB p99 handshake latency climbs from <5ms to 50–200ms during peak; CPU pegged >85% on LB nodes; clients see sporadic SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL and elevated upload initiation latency even though backends are healthy.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable TLS 1.3 with 0-RTT resumption; turn on session ticket keys rotated every 24h and shared across LB nodes; offload to dedicated AES-NI / QAT hardware; pre-warm a connection pool from sync clients with HTTP/2 multiplexing so many requests share one handshake. Scale LB horizontally on CPU, not connection count.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `lb.tls.handshake_p99_ms > 20` or `lb.cpu_util > 75%` for 5 min; track `lb.tls.resumption_rate` (target > 80%) — a drop indicates ticket key rotation or client-side churn.

bottlenecks.title: Connection concurrency cap vs long-poll /changes traffic
bottlenecks.trigger: The notification service uses long-poll HTTP on /changes?since=rev, and those connections traverse the LB. With 90M active devices and ~30s long-poll cycles, that's ~3M concurrent held connections across the LB fleet at steady state — the documented `concurrency: 50000` per LB node means we need at least 60 LB nodes just to hold the sockets, before any API traffic.
bottlenecks.symptom: New clients get connection refused or stuck in SYN_RECV during traffic spikes; ephemeral port exhaustion on LB → backend side; `accept` backlog overflows and kernel drops SYNs silently; multi-device sync latency balloons from ~1s to tens of seconds.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Route /changes long-poll traffic to a dedicated LB pool sized for connection count (not CPU), separate from the POST /files / PUT /commit pool. Use SO_REUSEPORT + multiple accept queues; increase `net.core.somaxconn` to 65535 and `nf_conntrack_max` to 4M; prefer WebSocket over long-poll to cut reconnect rate by 10x; use HTTP/2 on the client side so 3 devices per user share 1 TCP connection.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `lb.active_connections` per node (alert > 40K = 80% of cap), `lb.accept_queue_overflows` (any non-zero is bad), and `lb.ephemeral_port_util` (alert > 70%).

bottlenecks.title: Health-check flapping causes request re-routing storms
bottlenecks.trigger: 20+ stateless API replicas each handling ~400 concurrent requests. Any GC pause, deploy, or transient Redis/MySQL slowdown pushes /healthz past the typical 2s threshold and the LB yanks the replica out of rotation, shifting its ~35K/20 ≈ 1.75K QPS share onto the remaining pool — which can cascade as the now-overloaded peers also fail health checks.
bottlenecks.symptom: Periodic 2–10s windows of elevated 502/504s; LB access logs show sawtooth pattern of replicas going unhealthy/healthy; on-call sees 'API tier flapping' but individual replicas look fine when inspected; correlated upload commit failures.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use outlier detection (Envoy-style) with a minimum healthy-host floor (e.g. never eject more than 30% of pool); make /healthz cheap and dependency-free (don't check Redis/MySQL inline — use async liveness); configure slow-start mode so revived replicas get traffic ramped over 60s; set health check interval 5s with 3-failure threshold and 1.5s timeout to avoid spurious flips from single slow requests.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `lb.pool.healthy_host_count < 0.7 * total` or `lb.pool.ejection_rate > 2/min`; graph `lb.5xx_rate` correlated with `lb.pool.membership_changes`.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the load balancer is here for Google Drive The Drive API is stateless and runs as ~20 replicas so we can handle peak traffic and survive node failures. But clients — 100M daily active users across desktop agents, mobile apps, and browsers — only know one hostname like `api.drive.example.com`. Something has to sit at that hostname, terminate TLS for all those connections, and spread requests across the healthy API replicas. That's the load balancer's job here. It's also the only piece that can pull a sick replica out of rotation during a deploy or a GC pause without clients noticing. ## What happens without it If clients talked to a single API box directly, one deploy or one crash drops every sync agent on the planet — they'd all see connection refused and start reconnect storms. If you tried to round-robin via DNS instead, DNS TTLs are minutes long, so a dead replica keeps getting traffic for way too long, and you can't do health checks or TLS session resumption globally. Upload commits would fail intermittently, and support would see waves of "Drive is broken" tickets every time ops touches the API tier. ## The number Peak API load is ~35K QPS (10K writes + 25K reads). With ~20 API replicas, that's ~1.75K QPS per replica — fine, as long as traffic is actually balanced. If one replica gets 5K QPS and another gets 500 because of uneven client connections, the hot one tips over and cascades. The LB's least-connections tie-break is what keeps that distribution flat. ## Trade-off Every API request now pays an extra network hop and a TLS termination CPU cost at the edge — worth it for the ability to deploy and fail replicas without user-visible downtime.

api.name: Drive API (Metadata Service)
api.summary: Stateless service that owns file / folder metadata, ACLs, revisions, and coordinates between the block servers, notification service, and search indexer. This is the book's metadata service.

sections.heading: Endpoints
sections.body:
```
POST /files # create file metadata, return upload session
POST /files/:id/blocks # submit block hashes → returns which to upload
PUT /files/:id/commit # finalize upload (all blocks acknowledged)
GET /files/:id # metadata + block manifest
GET /files/:id/download # returns signed URLs per block
GET /files/:id/versions # list retained version history
POST /files/:id/share # grant/revoke permissions
GET /changes?since=rev # long-poll change feed (drives notification fan-in)
```

sections.heading: Upload negotiation
sections.body:
1. Client POSTs file metadata + block hash list
2. API creates file row (status=UPLOADING, rev=1)
3. API delegates dedup check to the block-server tier (bulk EXISTS against cloud storage / Bloom filter)
4. Replies with `{already_have: [hashes], need: [hashes + signed URLs]}`
5. Client uploads missing blocks via the block servers
6. Client calls commit → API validates all blocks present, updates manifest, flips status=READY, bumps rev, and hands off to the notification service + search indexer

sections.heading: Versioning + retention
sections.body: Every commit bumps `rev` and appends to a `versions` table. Retention policy keeps only the last N versions (e.g. 10) or T days (e.g. 30d) of active blocks — older versions' blocks decrement their refcount, and once refcount hits 0 the block is eligible for cold-tier migration or deletion. This is the book's 'storage space optimization via version limits'.

sections.heading: Horizontal scaling
sections.body: Stateless → scale on CPU and connection count. Peak 35K QPS / ~10ms avg → ~400 concurrent reqs per replica at safe utilization → 10 replicas minimum; run 20+ for regional redundancy.

gained: Tighter binary encoding saves ~40% on metadata round-trips
lost: Harder web client story (needs grpc-web gateway)
Less debuggable with curl

bottlenecks.title: Commit-path single-shard transaction contention on hot files
bottlenecks.trigger: Each /commit does a multi-statement txn: insert N blocks rows, append versions row, UPDATE files SET status, rev=rev+1. For collaborative docs (~1% shared, avg 3 collaborators) and rapid-save workflows (autosave every 30s), a single file_id can see 5–10 commits/min from different devices, all serialized on that row's shard. At peak 10K write QPS, a handful of hot files can monopolize an entire shard's txn slots.
bottlenecks.symptom: p99 commit latency climbs from ~20ms to hundreds of ms or seconds on specific files; sync agents report 'saving…' hangs; deadlock / lock-wait-timeout errors in MySQL logs concentrated on a few file_ids; cascading 5xx as API replicas fill their 3000-concurrency budget waiting on DB.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use optimistic concurrency: client sends `expected_rev` and API does `UPDATE files SET rev=rev+1 WHERE id=? AND rev=?` — on conflict return 409 and let client rebase. Keep the commit txn tight (single round-trip, batched INSERT for blocks). For truly hot collaborative files, route to a per-file serializer (single-writer queue keyed by file_id) so contention is bounded to one in-flight commit at a time without DB lock churn.
bottlenecks.detection: Histogram `api.commit.latency_ms` bucketed by file_id percentile; alert on p99 > 200ms for 5 min. Track `mysql.innodb.row_lock_waits` per shard and `api.commit.conflict_rate` (409s); any file_id appearing in top-10 by commit QPS for >10 min gets flagged.

bottlenecks.title: /changes long-poll holds API replica concurrency budget
bottlenecks.trigger: 90M active devices hold /changes?since=rev long-polls with ~30s cycles. Even if the notification service owns the socket, any long-poll that terminates at the API tier consumes one of the ~3000 concurrency slots per replica. 90M / (30s cycle) = 3M req/s of poll re-arms, and at 20 replicas that's 150K req/s/replica — far above the 400-concurrent safe utilization budget.
bottlenecks.symptom: API replicas show concurrency pinned at 3000 with most connections idle-waiting; POST /files and /commit latencies spike because write requests queue behind parked long-polls; accept queue overflows; unrelated endpoints (share, download) see 503s during traffic bumps.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Route /changes exclusively to the notification service tier (already in design) — never let it hit the stateless API pool. Enforce at the LB with path-based routing. For the API tier, cap per-route concurrency (e.g. /changes=0, /commit=2000, /files=1000) via envoy local rate limits. Use async I/O (Netty, asyncio, Go) so parked polls cost memory not a thread.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `api.concurrency_in_use` broken down by route; alert if /changes > 0 on API pool or if non-/changes routes exceed 70% of concurrency cap. Monitor `api.accept_queue_depth` and p99 latency per endpoint — if /commit p99 correlates with total concurrency (not its own QPS), long-polls are leaking in.

bottlenecks.title: Bulk dedup EXISTS check on large-file commits amplifies downstream calls
bottlenecks.trigger: A P99 1 GB file = 250 block hashes. Client POSTs all 250 hashes in one /files call; API fans out to the block-server dedup check, which hits Redis Bloom filter (fast) but Bloom false-positive rate ~1% → ~2–3 authoritative S3 HEAD calls per large file. At write peak 10K QPS with even 5% large-file uploads (500 QPS), that's ~125K Bloom ops/s + ~1250 S3 HEADs/s originating from API — and each API request now has 15–80ms service time (the sim's block-server range) blocking the API handler.
bottlenecks.symptom: POST /files latency tracks file size: small files 10ms, 1 GB files 200–500ms; API replicas see concurrency slots held open for the duration; sync agents report slow 'preparing upload' even though bytes haven't moved; S3 HEAD rate limits (5500/s/prefix) trip during upload bursts.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Make dedup resolution async from the metadata create: return 202 + upload session id immediately with hashes in PENDING state, resolve dedup in a background coroutine, and let client poll or receive via a streaming endpoint (gRPC or SSE). Batch HEAD requests across concurrent uploads at the block-server tier (coalesce 100ms windows). Tune Bloom filter to 0.1% FPR (8 GB instead of 5 GB) to cut authoritative lookups by 10x.
bottlenecks.detection: Histogram `api.files_post.latency_ms` bucketed by `block_count`; alert if p99 for >100-block requests exceeds 500ms. Track `api.dedup.bloom_fp_rate` (target <0.5%) and `s3.head.throttled_count` per prefix — any non-zero throttling during normal ops signals the amplification is hitting limits.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Drive API sits at the center of this design Google Drive isn't really a "file upload service" — it's a *sync* service. Every upload has to do five things atomically: check the user's quota, figure out which 4 MB blocks are already stored (dedup), write a new manifest with a bumped revision number, kick off thumbnail/OCR work, and tell the user's other devices something changed. Someone has to be the coordinator for all of that. The Drive API is that coordinator. The block servers move bytes, cloud storage holds bytes, the notification service pushes events — but none of them know *what a file is* or *who owns it*. Only the API does. ## What breaks without it If clients talked directly to cloud storage, there's no one to enforce "Alice can't read Bob's blocks," no one to bump `rev` transactionally so two devices editing the same file don't clobber each other, and no one to decide which blocks are dedup hits vs. need uploading. The user would see corrupted files after concurrent edits, random permission leaks, and "file saved" UI states that don't match what's actually in storage. The operator would see block storage growing without bound because nothing is refcounting or expiring old versions. ## The number Peak load is ~35K QPS (10K writes + 25K reads). With ~10ms average service time, each replica safely handles `10ms × concurrency ÷ 1000 = 400` concurrent requests → 35,000 ÷ 400 ≈ **88 requests/sec per replica**, so roughly 20 stateless replicas cover peak with headroom for a replica failing mid-deploy. ## Trade-off Making the API the single source of truth means every upload pays an extra round-trip before bytes flow — accepted in exchange for dedup, ACLs, and consistent revisions actually working.

meta.name: Metadata DB
meta.summary: Sharded relational store (MySQL / Spanner) for files, folders, permissions, and block manifests.

sections.heading: Schema
Sharding
sections.body: Shard by `owner_id` (or root folder id) so listing a user's files stays on one shard. Share-with-user is a cross-shard ACL lookup but low volume compared to listings.

sections.heading: Consistency
sections.body: Strong within a file (single-shard transactions for `rev` bumps); eventual across share-recipient shards. File rename/move is a single-shard txn; cross-shard move is a two-phase commit (rare).

sections.heading: Size
sections.body: 50B files * ~500 B row ≈ 25 TB. Block manifests dominate: 50B files * avg 5 blocks * 80 B ≈ 20 TB. ~100 shards at ~500 GB each on NVMe MySQL replicas.

gained: Global strong consistency without manual sharding
lost: Higher p99 due to TrueTime / consensus hops
Cost
Folder tree queries (LIST CHILDREN) are GSI-heavy
Transaction scope limited

bottlenecks.title: Hot-shard write amplification from block manifest inserts
bottlenecks.trigger: Every /commit inserts N rows into `blocks` (avg 5 per file, up to 250 for a 1 GB P99 file) plus a `versions` row plus a files UPDATE — all in one single-shard txn. At peak 10K write QPS with ~100 shards sharded by owner_id, a power-law user (enterprise tenant, shared team drive) concentrates thousands of commits/s on one shard, turning ~5 logical writes into 50K+ row inserts/s against a single MySQL primary whose sustained INSERT ceiling is ~20–30K rows/s on NVMe.
bottlenecks.symptom: One shard's replication lag grows from ms to tens of seconds; InnoDB history list length climbs; commit p99 on files owned by that shard jumps from 20ms to 500ms+; other shards look healthy, making it look like a 'random' slowdown; cross-device sync appears laggy only for some users.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Batch block inserts into a single multi-row INSERT (already implied but enforce <=1 round-trip per commit); move block manifests out of the row-store into a KV store keyed by (file_id, rev) — e.g. RocksDB/Cassandra — and keep only `files`/`versions`/`acls` in MySQL; add a per-tenant shard split when a shard exceeds 60% of write budget; use group commit (innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1 with binlog_group_commit_sync_delay=1000us) to amortize fsyncs.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-shard metrics: `mysql.com_insert` rate, `mysql.innodb.rows_inserted`, replication lag p99 (alert > 2s), and `commit_latency_ms` p99 tagged by shard_id. Alert if any shard sustains >70% of the fleet median write rate for 10 min (indicates hotspot before it tips over).

bottlenecks.title: Cross-shard share + folder-move operations scale poorly
bottlenecks.trigger: Sharding is by owner_id, but ~1% of 50B files are shared with avg 3 collaborators → 1.5B cross-shard ACL relationships to traverse on 'files shared with me' listings. Folder moves across owners require 2PC. At scale a single user viewing 'Shared with me' must fan out to potentially dozens of shards, and peak read QPS 25K means any of those queries that touches >5 shards turns into >125K shard-level QPS.
bottlenecks.symptom: 'Shared with me' view takes 2–10s to load for users with many collaborators; 2PC cross-shard moves occasionally time out and leave files in intermediate state; shard query amplification makes the metadata tier's effective QPS 5–10x higher than the user-facing QPS; tail latency p99 >> p50.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Denormalize: maintain an `acls_by_principal` table sharded by `principal_id` so 'shared with me' is a single-shard scan; use async replication to keep it eventually consistent with the authoritative `acls` table (accept ~1s staleness for share visibility); replace cross-shard 2PC moves with a copy-then-delete saga with a tombstone, logged in an outbox; cache 'shared with me' result sets in Redis with invalidation on share events.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `meta.query.shards_touched` histogram per API request (alert p99 > 5); separate SLO for `/files/shared-with-me` latency (target p99 < 300ms); monitor `meta.2pc.in_flight` and `meta.2pc.timeout_rate` (any non-zero timeout is an incident).

bottlenecks.title: Block manifest table dominates storage and index footprint per shard
bottlenecks.trigger: 50B files × avg 5 blocks × 80B chunk ref ≈ 20 TB of `blocks` rows, plus secondary indexes on (file_id, rev, idx). With 100 shards that's 200 GB/shard of manifest data alone, on top of ~250 GB/shard of `files` rows. InnoDB buffer pool on a 256 GB NVMe MySQL node can't hold both hot `files` and `blocks` indexes — buffer pool misses on block manifest lookups during downloads jump dramatically under load.
bottlenecks.symptom: Read latency on `GET /files/:id/download` is bimodal — fast (5ms, buffer-pool hit) or slow (30–80ms, disk read); buffer pool hit ratio drops from >99% to 94–96% during peak read traffic; download QPS gets throttled not by CPU but by disk IOPS on specific shards; old-version reads (rare, cold index pages) are especially bad.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Move `blocks` manifest to a separate storage engine optimized for append-heavy immutable data (RocksDB with tiered compaction, or a dedicated Cassandra cluster); partition `blocks` by rev so current-version reads hit only the hot partition; cache the current-rev manifest in Redis keyed by file_id (TTL 5 min, invalidate on commit) — a download just needs the current manifest, not the history.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor `mysql.innodb.buffer_pool_hit_ratio` per shard (alert < 98%); track `meta.blocks.query.p99_ms` separately from `meta.files.query.p99_ms`; watch disk read IOPS per shard vs. the instance's provisioned IOPS (alert > 70%).

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Metadata DB is here for Google Drive The bytes of your files live in cloud storage as opaque 4 MB blocks keyed by SHA-256 hash. But a block store has no idea that hash `a1b2c3…` is "page 2 of report.pdf, owned by Alice, in her /Work folder, revision 5, shared read-only with Bob." That structural knowledge — the folder tree, filenames, revisions, permissions, and the ordered list of block hashes that reconstitute each file — has to live somewhere queryable and transactional. That's the Metadata DB. It's what lets `/commit` bump a file's `rev` atomically so two devices editing at once don't corrupt each other, and it's what enforces "Alice owns this, Bob can read it" at every API call. ## What breaks without it Without a transactional metadata store, the block servers can still accept bytes, but nobody knows what belongs to whom. Users would see files randomly "disappear" (no folder tree to list them from), revisions would clobber each other on concurrent edits (no atomic `rev` bump), and permissions would be unenforceable (no ACL table to check). Operators would see block storage growing forever because there's no refcount to tell them which blocks are safe to delete. The API and the notification service both become useless — they have nothing authoritative to read from or invalidate against. ## The number The design stores **50B files × ~500 B/row ≈ 25 TB** for file rows, plus **50B × ~5 blocks × 80 B ≈ 20 TB** of block manifests — ~45 TB total. Sharded by `owner_id` across ~100 MySQL nodes, that's ~450 GB/shard on NVMe, comfortably within a single instance's buffer pool + disk, so a user's "list my files" stays a single-shard query returning in under 20ms. ## Trade-off Choosing a sharded SQL store gives per-file ACID transactions (critical for `rev` bumps) at the cost of painful cross-shard operations like "move this folder to another user's drive," which the design handles with rare two-phase commits.

cache.name: Metadata Cache
cache.summary: Hot-metadata cache: file rows, permission checks, and the block-hash existence bitmap.

sections.heading: What's cached
sections.body:
- `file:{id}` → file row JSON, TTL 5 min, invalidated on rev bump
- `acl:{user}:{file}` → role, TTL 1 min (permissions change often)
- `block_exists:{hash}` → Bloom filter for dedup fast-path so we don't hit cloud-storage index for every hash

sections.heading: Dedup bitmap
sections.body: The block-existence check is the hottest read on the write path. 10B known blocks * 32 B hash = 320 GB naive. We keep a Redis Bloom filter (redisbloom BF.ADD / BF.EXISTS) — false positives send ~0.1% of hashes to a slower authoritative lookup, but the filter fits in 5 GB with 1% FPR.

sections.heading: Eviction + failure
sections.body: `allkeys-lru` at 80% watermark. Cold cache → slower uploads (every hash hits cloud-storage index) but correctness intact.

lost: No Bloom filter module — would have to keep dedup filter elsewhere
No pub/sub for cache invalidation fan-out

bottlenecks.title: Bloom filter hot-key saturation on dedup fast-path
bottlenecks.trigger: Every upload hits BF.EXISTS once per block hash. Peak 10K write QPS × avg 5 blocks/file = 50K BF ops/s steady, spiking to ~125K/s when large files (P99 1 GB = 250 blocks) arrive in bursts. The Bloom filter is a single logical key `block_bf` of ~5 GB — all ops route to one Redis shard/primary, and RedisBloom BF.EXISTS is single-threaded per key.
bottlenecks.symptom: Redis CPU on the shard holding `block_bf` pegs at 100%; BF.EXISTS latency climbs from <1ms to 10–30ms; POST /files slows proportionally because the API blocks on dedup resolution; other Redis keys on the same shard (file rows, ACLs) see head-of-line latency spikes.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard the Bloom filter: partition by hash prefix (e.g. first byte → 256 logical filters) and distribute across a Redis Cluster so BF ops parallelize across nodes. Pipeline BF.EXISTS calls per upload (one MULTI with N hashes instead of N round-trips). Use client-side batching at the block-server tier to coalesce bursts. Alternative: replace RedisBloom with an in-process Bloom per block-server replica, refreshed from a durable source every few minutes (accepts slightly higher FPR for zero network cost).
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `redis.cpu_util{key_shard=block_bf} > 70%` or `redis.cmd.latency_p99{cmd=BF.EXISTS} > 5ms`. Track `api.dedup.bf_check_latency_ms` histogram — bimodal distribution signals shard saturation. Monitor per-shard op rate variance (coefficient of variation >0.5 means hotspot).

bottlenecks.title: Cache stampede on hot file invalidation after commit
bottlenecks.trigger: Every /commit invalidates `file:{id}` (5 min TTL). For collaborative files (~1% shared, avg 3 collaborators, but hot team-shared docs can see dozens of concurrent readers) a single rev bump drops the cache entry while tens-to-hundreds of devices are actively polling GET /files/:id. All miss simultaneously and stampede to the same MySQL shard. At peak 25K read QPS with even 100 hot files, that's thousands of concurrent SQL fetches for the same row.
bottlenecks.symptom: Sawtooth pattern on MySQL shard QPS correlated with commits on hot files; `meta.query.p99_ms` spikes from ~10ms to 100ms+ for seconds after each invalidation; API latency tail grows; in extreme cases shard connection pool exhausts and unrelated queries queue.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use request coalescing (single-flight) in the API: only one in-flight SQL fetch per file_id, others wait on the result. Replace hard invalidation with write-through: `SET file:{id}` to the new row inside the commit path rather than DELETE, eliminating the miss window. Add a short (100–500ms) negative-cache lock key to prevent thundering herd. For known-hot files, extend TTL and use pub/sub invalidations with staggered jitter.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `cache.miss_rate` per key prefix; alert on `file:*` miss rate > 5% sustained. Histogram `api.files_get.singleflight_wait_ms` — a rising p99 means coalescing is saving many callers (good signal it's needed). Watch MySQL `com_select` rate for sudden 10x bursts within 1s windows.

bottlenecks.title: Memory pressure from 50 GB working set approaching cluster capacity
bottlenecks.trigger: Design sizes Redis at ~50 GB for the hottest 10M file rows, plus 5 GB Bloom filter, plus `acl:{user}:{file}` entries (1 min TTL but huge keyspace — 100M DAU × avg files touched). Under normal traffic this fits, but during burst events (Monday morning sync storm, enterprise bulk-imports, or a viral shared file with millions of ACL checks) the working set can spike 2–3x and trigger allkeys-lru eviction on the file-row pool.
bottlenecks.symptom: Cache hit rate drops from >95% to 70–80% during bursts; MySQL read QPS doubles as evicted rows get re-fetched; Redis `used_memory` approaches `maxmemory`; eviction rate climbs and latency-sensitive keys (Bloom filter fragments, hot file rows) get evicted alongside cold ACL entries; API latency widens across the board.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Segment Redis by workload: separate clusters (or separate databases) for (a) file rows, (b) Bloom filter, (c) ACL cache — so eviction in one doesn't harm others. Set per-namespace memory caps with `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru` on the ACL pool only; use `noeviction` on the Bloom filter pool (it must never drop entries). Right-size with 40% headroom above observed p99 working set. Use Redis 7.x client-side caching (RESP3 tracking) to offload hot file-row reads to API replica memory, reducing Redis load.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `redis.used_memory_ratio > 0.75` per cluster; `redis.evicted_keys_per_sec > 100` sustained; `cache.hit_rate{namespace=file} < 0.9` for 5 min. Track working-set size via `MEMORY USAGE` sampling and project growth weekly.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why there's a Metadata Cache in Google Drive Every upload in Drive has to answer one question *fast*: "does this 4 MB block already exist somewhere in our storage?" That's the dedup check, and it's on the critical path of every single write. If we asked the Metadata DB (or worse, did an S3 HEAD) for every block hash, we'd crush the database — a 1 GB file alone asks this question 250 times before uploading a single byte. The cache exists because Drive's dedup promise ("don't re-upload what we already have") is *only* cheap if the existence check is basically free. It also caches the file row itself, so when your phone polls "what changed?" after your laptop saves, we don't hit MySQL for every poll. ## What happens without it Cold cache means every dedup check and every file lookup hits the sharded MySQL tier. Users experience laggy "Preparing upload…" spinners because each of the 250 block hashes in a large file now takes a 5–20ms DB round-trip instead of a 1ms Redis check. Operators see MySQL CPU pinned, replication lag climbing, and the Drive API tier's concurrency budget filling with threads parked on DB calls — which cascades into 5xx on *unrelated* endpoints like share and download. ## The number The design estimates **10B known blocks**. Storing all hashes naively as a set would be 10B × 32 B = **320 GB** — way too much for memory. A Bloom filter with 1% false-positive rate compresses that to **~5 GB**, easily fitting in Redis, and the 1% of false positives that fall through to an authoritative S3 HEAD are rare enough to not matter. With peak writes at 10K QPS × ~5 blocks/file = 50K dedup checks/sec, serving those from Redis at ~1ms each is the difference between a healthy system and a melting one. ## Trade-off The designer accepted eventual consistency on cached file rows (5-min TTL, invalidated on commit) — a brief window where a stale read is possible — in exchange for keeping MySQL alive under 25K read QPS.

block.name: Block Servers
block.summary: The book's block-server tier: splits files into blocks, compresses, encrypts, and uploads blocks to cloud storage. Also answers the dedup-existence query and issues per-block signed URLs.

sections.heading: Responsibilities (book's 4 steps)
sections.body:
For each file, the block server:
1. Splits the file into 4 MB blocks (fixed chunking)
2. Compresses each block (zstd / snappy)
3. Encrypts each block (per-user key, envelope encryption)
4. Uploads the block to cloud storage using its SHA-256 hash as the object key
On the download path, the reverse happens: fetch block by hash, decrypt, decompress, concatenate.

sections.heading: Delta sync support
sections.body: When the client sends its new block-hash list, the block server does a bulk EXISTS check against cloud storage (Bloom filter → authoritative HEAD). It returns `{hash, action: skip | upload, url?: signed_put_url}` so the client only transfers blocks whose hash is not already stored globally. This is both dedup (across users) and delta sync (within a user's own revisions).

sections.heading: Why a separate tier from the API
sections.body:
- Different scaling profile: block server is bandwidth-heavy (the bytes flow through if we don't use client-direct presigned PUTs), API is request-heavy
- Holds the cloud-storage IAM credentials + per-user KMS encryption keys — isolates those secrets from the broader API tier
- Can be deployed close to users (regional block servers) to reduce upload latency

sections.heading: Dedup win
sections.body: Empirical: 30% of bytes in Drive-like workloads are duplicate (shared attachments, re-uploaded photos, near-duplicate docs). Dedup saves ~3 PB/day of egress for a 10 PB/day raw workload.

gained: Shift-resistant dedup — inserting a byte at the front of a file still matches later blocks
lost: Rolling hash compute cost (Rabin-Karp) on client
Harder to reason about block-size bounds

bottlenecks.title: Bloom filter + cloud storage HEAD storm on bulk dedup checks
bottlenecks.trigger: Peak 10K write QPS × avg 5 blocks/file = 50K dedup checks/s steady, spiking to 125K/s when P99 1 GB files (250 blocks) arrive in bursts. Bloom false-positive rate of 1% on 50K ops/s = 500 authoritative S3 HEAD calls/s, which can concentrate on a small number of 2-byte key prefixes and hit S3's 5,500 HEAD/s/prefix limit during bursty uploads.
bottlenecks.symptom: POST /files latency for large files climbs from ~50ms to 500ms+; S3 returns 503 SlowDown errors on HEAD requests; block-server concurrency (3000 cap) fills with requests parked on HEAD calls; small-file uploads queue behind large-file dedup resolution; sync agents display extended 'Preparing upload…' with no bytes flowing.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Tune Bloom filter to 0.1% FPR (trade 5 GB → ~8 GB memory for 10x fewer authoritative lookups); batch/coalesce HEAD requests across concurrent uploads in 50–100ms windows; add a second-tier in-process LRU cache of recently-confirmed hashes per block-server replica (1M entries, ~100 MB) to absorb repeat checks; distribute cloud-storage keys with the 2-byte hash prefix scheme already in the design to spread HEAD load across S3 partitions; pipeline BF.EXISTS calls into a single Redis MULTI per upload.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `block.dedup.head_qps > 1000` sustained or `s3.head.throttled_count > 0` for any prefix; histogram `block.dedup.resolution_latency_ms` bucketed by block_count (alert p99 > 300ms for >100-block requests); track `block.bloom.fp_rate` (target <0.5%) and `block.dedup.head_cache_hit_rate` (target >90%).

bottlenecks.title: Per-user KMS envelope-encryption key ops saturate on burst uploads
bottlenecks.trigger: Block server encrypts every uploaded block with a per-user data key via envelope encryption. At 12 GB/s aggregate upload bandwidth ÷ 4 MB blocks ≈ 3,000 blocks/s encrypted globally, each requiring a KMS Decrypt call on the wrapped data key (or a cache lookup). A single enterprise tenant doing a bulk migration (millions of files) can drive 500+ blocks/s for one user_id, and KMS per-key QPS limits (e.g. AWS KMS 10K RPS shared, per-key much lower) combined with cache misses create a hot-key throttle.
bottlenecks.symptom: Upload throughput for specific users/tenants caps far below available bandwidth; KMS ThrottlingException in logs; block-server workers block in encrypt for 100–500ms waiting on KMS; bulk imports stall; other users' uploads degrade because block-server concurrency budget is consumed by parked encryption threads.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cache the unwrapped data key in-memory per block-server replica with a TTL (e.g. 15 min) and a per-user LRU (100K entries) so a tenant's burst hits KMS once, not once per block; use hierarchical keys (per-user KEK unwraps a per-upload-session DEK) so one KMS call amortizes over an entire file's 250 blocks; pre-warm keys on /files creation so the /commit block-upload path is never the first KMS touch; request KMS quota increase and distribute across regional KMS endpoints.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `kms.throttled_requests > 0` or `block.encrypt.latency_p99_ms > 50`; track `block.kms.cache_hit_rate` (target >99%) and `block.kms.calls_per_block` (target <0.01 with caching); per-user histogram of encrypt latency to spot hot tenants before they trip global quota.

bottlenecks.title: Regional block-server bandwidth bottleneck proxying large uploads
bottlenecks.trigger: Design targets 12 GB/s aggregate upload bandwidth. If block servers compress+encrypt in-line (not client-side) before forwarding to cloud storage, the bytes flow through the block-server fleet — a regional block-server pod handling its share of traffic must sustain ~200–500 MB/s NIC throughput per pod. A 1 GB file upload pins a block-server worker for 10–30s at full NIC, and with 3000-concurrency per replica, a few dozen simultaneous large-file uploads saturate a 10 Gbps NIC before concurrency limits trigger.
bottlenecks.symptom: Block-server NIC utilization pegs at 90%+ during peak; upload throughput for individual files drops from expected 40 MB/s to 5–10 MB/s; cross-region latency grows (block server in us-east, cloud storage in us-west); large-file uploads appear to make progress but at fraction of client's link speed; noisy-neighbor effects where one user's big upload slows others on the same pod.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use client-direct presigned PUT URLs (already in the dedup response) so bytes bypass the block-server data path entirely — block servers only coordinate, not proxy; when server-side encrypt is required for compliance, run block servers in the same region/AZ as the target cloud-storage bucket to avoid cross-region hops; add per-upload bandwidth fairness (token bucket per user_id) so one bulk user can't starve others on the same pod; scale block-server pods on NIC utilization, not request count.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor `block.nic.util_pct` per pod (alert >75% sustained 5 min); track `block.upload.goodput_mbps` per active upload — bimodal distribution with a low-throughput cluster indicates saturation; alert on `block.upload.p99_duration_ms` for 1 GB files exceeding 30s (expected ~25s at 40 MB/s); compare client-reported upload rate vs block-server egress rate to detect proxying inefficiency.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Block Servers are here for Google Drive In Drive, the API tier handles *metadata* (filenames, folders, permissions, revisions) — small, transactional stuff. But actual file bytes are a completely different beast: a single 1 GB video is 250 blocks of 4 MB each, and the system ingests ~12 GB/s aggregate across all users. Mixing those two workloads into one service would be a disaster. The Block Servers exist to own the bytes path — they answer "does this SHA-256 hash already exist globally?" (dedup), compress and encrypt each block, and hand the client pre-signed URLs to shove bytes directly into cloud storage. They also hold the IAM credentials and per-user KMS keys, so those secrets stay isolated from the broader API tier. ## What happens without it If the API tier did all this inline, every /commit would block for seconds while the API hashed, encrypted, and uploaded 250 blocks. The API's concurrency budget (3000 slots per replica) would fill with parked threads, and completely unrelated requests like "list my folder" or "share this file" would start returning 503s. Operators would see API CPU pegged, metadata DB connections starved, and dedup effectively broken because there's no dedicated tier to maintain the Bloom filter fast-path. ## The number The design calls out a **30% dedup ratio** on ~10 PB/day of raw uploads. That's ~3 PB/day of bytes *never transferred* because the Block Server checked hashes first and said "skip." Without that tier doing the existence check at 50K blocks/sec, you'd pay egress *and* storage for all 10 PB. ## Trade-off The designer accepted an extra service to operate (and an extra network hop on the coordination path) in exchange for keeping the hot metadata API responsive under bursty multi-gigabyte uploads.

blob.name: Cloud Storage (Hot Blocks)
blob.summary: Content-addressed object store keyed by block SHA-256; the authoritative home of every active 4 MB block.

sections.heading: Layout
sections.body: Key = `blocks/{hash[0:2]}/{hash[2:4]}/{hash}` — the 2-byte prefixes are for S3 request-distribution so hot prefixes don't throttle.

sections.heading: Durability
sections.body: 11 9's (S3-standard-equivalent). Cross-region replication for disaster recovery. Erasure-coded (10+4 RS) under the hood for 1.4x storage overhead instead of 3x replication.

sections.heading: Refcounting
sections.body: Dedup means a block may be referenced by millions of files. Delete is a *decrement* on a separate refcount table (Cassandra). When refcount reaches 0 AND 7 days have passed (tombstone window), the block is moved to cold storage (if it might still be resurrected via version history) or deleted.

sections.heading: Hot-tier sizing
sections.body: Only blocks touched in the last 90 days live here. This is typically 20–30% of total stored bytes — the rest tiers down.

lost: Cross-cloud egress fees if compute is not on GCP

gained: No per-GB cloud pricing at multi-PB scale
lost: Ops heavy: monitors, OSDs, CRUSH map tuning
Weaker multi-region story

bottlenecks.title: S3 prefix request-rate throttling on hot hash ranges
bottlenecks.trigger: Peak upload path drives ~3,000 block PUTs/s (12 GB/s ÷ 4 MB) plus ~125K HEAD/s during dedup bursts for P99 1 GB files (250 blocks each). S3 caps at 3,500 PUT/s and 5,500 GET+HEAD/s per prefix. Even with the 2-byte prefix scheme (`blocks/{hash[0:2]}/...`) giving 65,536 prefixes, real SHA-256 distribution has micro-hotspots when bulk workloads hash-collide on leading bytes, and small deployments may only populate a fraction of prefixes.
bottlenecks.symptom: S3 returns 503 SlowDown on PUT/HEAD; block-server workers retry with exponential backoff consuming their 3,000-concurrency budget; upload p99 climbs from ~80ms to seconds; cascading failures where dedup HEAD storms crowd out actual block PUTs; uploads appear to stall with no obvious cause on Drive's side.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use full 2-byte prefix (not just first byte) to guarantee 65K partitions; monitor per-prefix QPS and pre-warm S3 partitioning by filing a support ticket before launch / bulk migrations; add client-side request hedging with jitter; implement adaptive retry with circuit breaker per-prefix at the block-server tier; for truly hot shared blocks (viral file), add a CloudFront/CDN read-through layer so HEAD/GET don't all hit S3 directly.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `s3.5xx_rate{code=503,op=PUT|HEAD} > 0.1%` for any 1-min window; track per-prefix QPS histogram (top-100 prefixes) and alert if any exceeds 2,500 PUT/s or 4,000 HEAD/s (70% of ceiling); watch `block.retry_rate` for sustained >1% as leading indicator.

bottlenecks.title: Refcount table (Cassandra) contention on highly-dedup'd blocks
bottlenecks.trigger: Dedup means a popular block (corporate logo, shared template, viral PDF page) can be referenced by millions of files. Every /commit increments the refcount for each block's hash; every delete decrements. At 10K write QPS × 5 blocks/file = 50K refcount ops/s, and hot blocks can see 1,000+ concurrent increments on the same partition key. Cassandra counters are notoriously expensive (read-before-write internally) and hot-partition contention can crash tombstone/compaction cycles.
bottlenecks.symptom: Commit latency spikes for files containing popular blocks; Cassandra hot-partition warnings in logs; counter drift (observed refcount ≠ actual references) after repair operations; block GC either deletes live blocks (data loss!) or fails to reclaim orphaned blocks (storage bloat); compaction falls behind on counter CF.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Replace counters with an append-only event log (insert a row per ref/unref with timestamp) and compute refcount asynchronously via a periodic rollup job — trades real-time accuracy for massively better write throughput; shard counters by (hash, random_bucket_of_16) and SUM on read; enforce a 7-day tombstone window before any delete so transient counter lag can't cause data loss; for extreme hot blocks, short-circuit: if refcount > 1000 skip GC entirely (the block will never be orphaned in practice).
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `cassandra.partition.size{table=refcounts} > 100MB` (hot partition); track `cassandra.counter.write_latency_p99 > 50ms`; monitor `blob.gc.orphan_candidates` vs `blob.gc.actually_deleted` ratio — divergence signals counter drift; run periodic audit job comparing counter sum to SELECT COUNT(*) from manifests.

bottlenecks.title: Cross-region replication lag breaks durability SLO during regional bursts
bottlenecks.trigger: 12 GB/s aggregate ingest with cross-region replication for DR. S3 CRR typically replicates within 15 minutes for 99% of objects but can lag hours during ingest bursts (e.g., enterprise onboarding bulk-uploading 100 TB). Until a block is replicated, a regional failure loses that block — and manifests in the Metadata DB reference blocks by hash assuming they're durable/available.
bottlenecks.symptom: Regional outage exposes 'missing block' errors on downloads for recently-uploaded files; RPO SLO (e.g., <1 min) violated in post-mortem; during normal ops CRR backlog metric climbs into millions of objects; DR drill reveals gap between what metadata claims exists and what's replicated.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use S3 Replication Time Control (RTC) with 15-min SLA guarantee (extra cost but contractual); for critical customers, synchronous dual-region write at the block-server tier before /commit acknowledges (trades ~50ms latency for zero-RPO durability); expose replication status per block in metadata and have API reject downloads of unreplicated blocks during regional failover; pre-warm replication bandwidth via S3 Multi-Region Access Points.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `s3.replication.backlog_objects > 100000` or `s3.replication.lag_p99_minutes > 20`; track `s3.replication.rtc_sla_breach_count` (should be zero with RTC enabled); periodic DR drill measuring actual RPO against SLO; per-region `blob.unreplicated_blocks` count exposed as SLI.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Cloud Storage is here for Google Drive Drive's whole design is built on splitting files into 4 MB blocks and identifying each one by its SHA-256 hash. Those blocks have to actually live *somewhere* — something that can hold petabytes, survive disk failures, and serve any block by its hash key on demand. That's what the Cloud Storage tier is. Crucially, it's *content-addressed*: the block's hash IS its storage key, which is what makes dedup work. When two different users upload the same PDF page, they both compute the same SHA-256, the block server sees the key already exists, and the second upload becomes a no-op. No central database is tracking "who has what bytes" — the storage layout itself enforces dedup. ## What breaks without it If you tried to stuff 4 MB blocks into the Metadata DB as BLOBs, you'd blow up MySQL's buffer pool on the first large user and every file read would compete with ACL lookups and revision bumps. The user would see downloads crawl and sync stall; the operator would see MySQL disk IOPS pegged and replication lag climbing into minutes. The Block Servers and Upload Workers would have nowhere to route bytes, so even small uploads would fail. ## The number The design estimates **10 PB raw, ~7 PB after dedup** across 50B files, at **12 GB/s aggregate ingest**. At 12 GB/s, a single MySQL node (maybe 500 MB/s sustained write) would be swamped 24x over. Object storage scales horizontally across thousands of disks, and the 2-byte hash prefix (`blocks/{hash[0:2]}/...`) spreads load across 65,536 partitions so no single prefix gets hammered. ## Trade-off Separating bytes from metadata means two systems to keep consistent (an orphaned block or a dangling manifest pointer is now possible), which the design handles with refcounting plus a 7-day tombstone window before any delete.

cold.name: Cold Storage / Offline Backup
cold.summary: Low-cost tier (S3 Glacier / GCS Archive) holding old versions, infrequently-accessed blocks, and the offline backup copy the book calls out for disaster recovery.

sections.heading: What lives here (storage space optimization)
sections.body:
- Blocks untouched for 90+ days
- Version-history blocks older than the retention window (e.g. beyond the last 10 revisions)
- A cross-region offline backup of every block for disaster recovery — the book explicitly separates 'backup' storage from active cloud storage so a regional outage / ransomware event doesn't lose user data.

sections.heading: Access pattern
sections.body: Reads are rare (< 0.1% of request volume). Retrieval is either 'Instant Retrieval' (ms, slightly higher per-GB cost) or 'Standard' (minutes, cheapest). Drive-style services use Instant Retrieval for user-facing access so reading an old version feels normal.

sections.heading: Space savings
sections.body: Cold tier is ~4x cheaper per GB than hot. 70% of bytes tier down over time → ~3x overall storage cost reduction on top of the 30% saved from dedup.

sections.heading: Re-hydration
sections.body: On read, a cold block is copied back to hot storage and served. The refcount-based GC keeps it hot while it's being actively used, then drops it back down.

lost: Minute-to-hour retrieval latency breaks interactive 'view old version' UX

bottlenecks.title: Retrieval latency spikes when users browse old version history
bottlenecks.trigger: Version-history retention drops blocks older than the last 10 revs or 30 days to cold tier. When a user opens 'Version history' on a heavily-edited doc (say, 50 past revisions × avg 5 blocks = 250 cold blocks), even Instant Retrieval adds 30–200ms per block vs <80ms from hot, and if Glacier Flexible Retrieval is used the wait is minutes-to-hours. Concurrent users browsing history on large docs amplify this — 0.1% of 25K read QPS = 25 cold-tier RPS steady, spiking 10x on a viral/legal-hold event.
bottlenecks.symptom: Version history UI shows spinners for seconds; downloading an old rev of a 1 GB file takes 30s–several minutes instead of <5s; on-call sees `blob.cold.get_latency_p99` in the seconds range; users file tickets claiming 'old versions are broken' or 'my file is stuck restoring'.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval (not Flexible/Deep Archive) for anything user-facing; pre-hydrate cold blocks to hot on first version-history open with read-through caching (keep re-hydrated blocks hot for 24h via refcount bump); parallelize cold GETs per-file (fan out all 250 blocks concurrently); show progressive UI with per-block progress instead of blocking on full file; for Flexible Retrieval tier, use bulk restore API and notify via notification service when ready.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `blob.cold.get_latency_p99_ms > 500` for Instant tier or any unexpected use of Flexible tier on user-facing path; track `cold.rehydrate_rate` and `cold.rehydrate_queue_depth`; SLO per-operation histogram on 'open version history' end-to-end latency (target p95 < 2s).

bottlenecks.title: Refcount race during hot→cold migration causes data loss or orphan bloat
bottlenecks.trigger: Migration is a move (copy to cold, verify, delete from hot), and runs concurrently with user uploads that may reference the exact same hash via dedup. If a new /commit increments refcount on a block *while* the sweeper has decided to migrate it (refcount=0 check happened 100ms earlier), the delete-from-hot can win the race and leave a manifest pointing at a cold-only or missing block. With ~3,000 block writes/s and dedup ratio 30%, thousands of blocks/day are candidates with non-trivial resurrection probability.
bottlenecks.symptom: Downloads intermittently return 404 or stall on re-hydration for blocks that the manifest says should exist; post-incident audit finds files referencing hashes that exist only in cold; storage bloat from tombstoned-but-not-deleted blocks if the sweeper errs cautiously; in worst case, user reports 'my file is corrupted' after a save.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce a 7-day tombstone window (already in design) + double-check refcount with a compare-and-swap at delete time; use S3 versioning on the hot tier so a delete is recoverable; migrate via COPY-then-mark-cold rather than COPY-then-DELETE — keep both copies for the tombstone window; make the block-server dedup path check cold tier too (HEAD on cold if hot miss) so a racing commit still finds the block; write migration events to an outbox that the dedup fast-path observes.
bottlenecks.detection: Periodic audit job: for every cold block, confirm no manifest in Metadata DB references it as hot-only; alert on `blob.download.block_not_found_rate > 0.0001%`; track `cold.migration.race_detected` counter (any non-zero value is an incident); dual-tier HEAD check latency as a sentinel for dedup correctness.

bottlenecks.title: Migration throughput cannot keep up with hot-tier churn, starving cost savings
bottlenecks.trigger: Design targets 70% of 7 PB (~5 PB) to tier down for ~3x storage cost reduction. At steady state with 1 PB/day ingest and version retention kicking in after 30 days, the sweeper must move ~700 TB/day (≈8 GB/s sustained) from hot to cold, including the object copy, verification, manifest update, and hot delete. S3 COPY is ~1 Gbps/prefix and cross-region copy to a cold bucket amplifies this; the worker fleet (200 pods, sim shows 50–500ms/task) is sized for upload post-processing, not bulk migration.
bottlenecks.symptom: Hot-tier storage grows unboundedly despite retention policy; monthly storage bill climbs ~3x expected; sweep backlog (versions eligible for migration but still on hot) grows into millions; on-call sees `cold.migration.backlog_age_p99_days > 45` (should be near 30); eventually capacity planning forces emergency hot-tier expansion.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use S3 Lifecycle policies for the common case (automatic tier transition after N days) instead of worker-driven copies — offloads 90% of migrations to AWS; dedicated migration worker pool with horizontal autoscaling on backlog depth; batch migrations by hash prefix to exploit S3 parallelism across 65K prefixes; use S3 Batch Operations for bulk transitions (millions of objects per job); measure and budget migration bandwidth as a first-class SLO separate from user-facing I/O.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `cold.migration.backlog_size > 10M objects` or `cold.migration.oldest_pending_age_days > 40`; track `hot_tier.bytes_total` growth rate vs ingest rate — divergence signals migration falling behind; weekly report on actual vs target cost-tier distribution (target: 70% cold / 30% hot).

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Cold Storage is here for Google Drive Drive promises two things that fight each other: "your files are safe forever, including old versions" and "storage is cheap enough for us to give you 15 GB free." Every time you hit save on a doc, that's a new revision, and those revisions pile up fast — a single user rewriting the same report 100 times would store 100 copies of mostly-identical blocks. The hot cloud-storage tier is optimized for fast reads of *active* blocks, but paying hot-tier prices for a block nobody has touched in 6 months is wasted money. Cold storage exists to hold old-version blocks and the disaster-recovery backup copy at ~4x lower cost per GB, while keeping them retrievable in milliseconds when a user does click "version history." ## What happens without it Without a cold tier, every historical revision sits on hot storage forever. The operator sees the storage bill grow roughly linearly with user-tenure — doubling every couple of years even if active usage is flat. Eventually someone in finance forces an aggressive retention policy ("we only keep 3 versions now") and users lose the ability to recover a file they edited last month. The Metadata DB and block refcounting machinery also bloat, since every one of those rarely-read blocks still consumes a row and an index entry in the hot path. ## The number The design stores **~7 PB** after dedup and estimates **70% of bytes tier down** over time. That's ~5 PB moved to cold at roughly 1/4 the price — saving ~75% of storage cost on 5 PB, or a ~3x overall reduction stacked on top of the 30% dedup win. ## Trade-off The designer accepted extra complexity (a migration pipeline, refcount-aware GC, and occasional re-hydration latency) in exchange for making unlimited version history economically viable.

uploadq.name: Upload Queue
uploadq.summary: Kafka topic of commit events that drives async post-processing (indexing, thumbnails, malware scan, cold-tier migration decisions).

sections.heading: Message shape
sections.body:
```
{ file_id, owner_id, rev, block_count, mime_type, size_bytes, ts }
```
Produced by the API after `/commit` succeeds.

sections.heading: Partitioning
sections.body: Partition by `owner_id` so a single user's events stay ordered (important for rapid rename/delete sequences).

sections.heading: Consumers
sections.body:
- Search indexer (filename + content OCR)
- Thumbnail generator (images / PDFs)
- Malware scanner
- Version-retention sweeper (moves expired revisions' blocks toward cold storage)
- Notification fan-out for collaborators (the notification service also subscribes here so it can push multi-device updates)

lost: No ordering across partitions
14d retention cap (no replay for re-indexing)

bottlenecks.title: Per-user partition hot-spotting from bulk imports and power tenants
bottlenecks.trigger: Partitioning by owner_id keeps a user's events ordered, but an enterprise tenant or team-drive owner doing a bulk migration can drive thousands of commits/s onto one partition. At peak 10K write QPS globally and ~32 partitions (hash(owner_id)%32), a single power tenant at 1K commits/s slams one partition while 31 others idle — a single Kafka partition's practical throughput cap (~10–50 MB/s, limited by the single consumer thread per partition) is blown by the downstream worker's 50–500ms processing time.
bottlenecks.symptom: Consumer lag on one partition grows into millions of messages while others are near zero; thumbnails / OCR / search indexing show up hours late for that tenant; `kafka.consumer.lag` graphed per-partition looks like a spike; on-call sees 'search is broken for Acme Corp' tickets but the fleet looks healthy in aggregate.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use a composite key `(owner_id, file_id % 8)` to sub-shard power users across 8 partitions while preserving per-file ordering (ordering per owner is not actually required — rename/delete sequences are per-file); add an automatic tenant-split policy that detects owner_ids exceeding 5% of partition throughput and routes them to a dedicated high-fanout topic; scale consumer group horizontally only helps if partitions are balanced — enforce with partition-count >> consumer-count (e.g. 256 partitions for 200 workers).
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `kafka.partition.lag{topic=file-committed} > 100000` for any single partition while fleet p50 lag < 1000 (imbalance signal); track per-partition msg-rate coefficient of variation (alert >0.5); top-10 owner_id by produce rate dashboard refreshed every 5 min.

bottlenecks.title: Consumer lag cascade from slow large-file post-processing
bottlenecks.trigger: Workers take 50–500ms per event and large files (>100 MB) pin a worker for 10–30s doing OCR/thumbnails. At peak 10K commits/s feeding ~200 worker pods, even a modest 5% large-file rate (500/s) requires 500 × 20s = 10,000 worker-seconds/s of capacity — 50x the fleet's steady-state throughput. Kafka retains 7d but lag buildup at 10K/s fills a single partition's backlog with millions of messages in minutes.
bottlenecks.symptom: Consumer group lag climbs monotonically during business-hour peaks; thumbnails appear minutes-to-hours after upload; search results miss recent files; `kafka.consumer.records-lag-max` alerts fire; worker fleet CPU is NOT pegged (workers are I/O-bound waiting on cloud-storage reads), masking the real capacity shortage.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Split into separate topics for small-file and large-file events (producer routes by size_bytes >100MB); dedicated large-file consumer group with its own autoscaling policy; use Kafka consumer `max.poll.records=1` on large-file lane so slow processing doesn't block heartbeats and trigger rebalances; budget worker fleet on p99 processing time × expected large-file rate, not average.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `kafka.consumer.lag_seconds{topic=file-committed} > 60` (p95 processing SLO); separate SLI for lag by message-size bucket; track `worker.processing_duration_ms` p99 broken down by mime_type and file_size bucket; watch for rebalance storms via `kafka.consumer.rebalance.rate`.

bottlenecks.title: Multi-consumer fan-out amplifies effective throughput requirement
bottlenecks.trigger: Five independent consumer groups subscribe to `file-committed`: search indexer, thumbnail generator, malware scanner, retention sweeper, and notification service. Each consumes the full 10K msg/s stream independently — effective broker read throughput is 5× produce rate = 50K msg/s reads. At ~1 KB/msg that's 50 MB/s fan-out read bandwidth per partition leader, and any new consumer group (analytics, compliance audit) adds another 10K/s of reads.
bottlenecks.symptom: Broker network-out saturates before produce-side limits; adding a new consumer group noticeably degrades existing consumers' fetch latency; broker disk page cache miss rate climbs as working set exceeds RAM; under-provisioned brokers become the bottleneck even though messages-per-second looks modest.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Size broker fleet on fan-out-adjusted throughput (produce_rate × consumer_group_count), not raw produce rate; enable Kafka tiered storage or rely on page cache with enough RAM to hold 5–10 min of topic data (at 10K/s × 1KB × 600s = 6 GB/broker minimum); use compact topic partitioning so each consumer group reads from a partition-leader that's geographically close; consider a fan-out pattern where one relay consumer splits to per-use-case topics if new consumer groups are frequent.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `kafka.broker.network.out.bytes_per_sec > 70%` of NIC capacity; track `kafka.broker.page_cache_hit_ratio < 0.95`; dashboard of consumer-group count per topic and bytes-read-per-group; alert when a new consumer group lands without capacity review.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why there's an Upload Queue in Google Drive When a user hits save on a 50 MB presentation, the `/commit` call has to return fast — the UI is waiting, the sync agent is blocking, and other devices expect a notification within ~1 second. But there's a pile of work that *should* happen after every upload: generate thumbnails at 3 resolutions, run a malware scan, extract text for search (OCR on PDFs, parsing Office docs), evaluate whether old versions should tier down to cold storage, and fan out to collaborators. Doing all of that inline would turn a 300ms commit into a 10-second wait. The Upload Queue exists so `/commit` can write the metadata row, drop one small event onto Kafka, and return — while a separate worker fleet chews through the expensive stuff asynchronously. ## What breaks without it If the API did this synchronously, every upload would block on ClamAV and Tika. Users would see "Saving…" spinners for 5-30 seconds on large files. Worse, if the thumbnail service had a bad deploy, commits themselves would start failing — one flaky downstream takes out the write path. Operators would watch API replica concurrency (3,000 slots) fill with threads parked on OCR, then watch unrelated endpoints like `/share` start returning 503s. ## The number Peak write load is ~10K commits/sec, and workers take 50-500ms per file (large files up to 30s). At 10K/sec × 500ms average = 5,000 worker-seconds per real second — you physically cannot do this inline on the API tier without a 5,000× concurrency multiplier. The queue absorbs bursts and lets ~200 worker pods drain at their own pace. ## Trade-off Thumbnails and search indexing become eventually-consistent (visible seconds-to-minutes after upload) in exchange for a fast, reliable commit path.

worker.name: Upload Worker
worker.summary: Consumer fleet that runs post-upload processing: thumbnail, malware scan, text extraction for search, and cold-tier migration.

sections.heading: Pipeline
sections.body:
1. Fetch blocks from cloud storage (stream-reassemble)
2. If image/PDF → render thumbnails at 128/512/2048 px, write to thumbnail bucket
3. ClamAV / Yara scan → on hit, mark file quarantined in metadata
4. Tika/OCR text extraction → emit to search indexer
5. Apply version-retention policy: if a retired version's blocks are now orphaned, migrate to cold storage
6. Update file status to `READY`

sections.heading: Concurrency
sections.body: ~200 worker pods, each handling 1–2 files concurrently. Large files (> 100 MB) pin a worker for 10–30 seconds — we keep a small-file lane and a large-file lane to avoid head-of-line blocking.

sections.heading: Failure handling
sections.body: Retry 3x with exponential backoff; persistent failure routes to DLQ and raises a low-sev alert. File remains usable (you can still download), just missing thumbnails / search.

alternatives.name: AWS Lambda triggered by S3 events

gained: Autoscales to zero, no fleet to manage
lost: 15 min hard timeout breaks large-file processing
Cold starts hurt tail latency

bottlenecks.title: Large-file processing pins workers and starves small-file queue
bottlenecks.trigger: Workers take 50–500ms per small file but large files (>100 MB, up to P99 1 GB) pin a worker for 10–30s doing OCR/thumbnail/malware scan. At peak 10K commits/s feeding ~200 worker pods with concurrency 1–2, even 5% large files = 500/s needing ~20s each = 10,000 worker-seconds/s of demand — 25× the fleet's ~400 worker-seconds/s capacity (200 pods × 2 concurrent).
bottlenecks.symptom: Small-file thumbnails that should appear in <1s take minutes; Kafka consumer lag on the large-file partition grows into millions; worker CPU looks modest (I/O-bound on cloud-storage reads) masking the real shortage; users complain 'search doesn't find my file I just uploaded'.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce strict lane separation: route size_bytes>100MB to a dedicated Kafka topic with its own consumer group and autoscaling policy on lag (not CPU); set max.poll.records=1 on the large-file lane so slow processing doesn't trigger rebalances; size the large-file fleet on p99 duration × expected rate (e.g. 30s × 500/s = 15K worker-seconds → ~500 dedicated pods with concurrency=1); stream-process rather than download-then-process to cut per-file wall time.
bottlenecks.detection: Separate SLI for `worker.processing_duration_ms` p99 bucketed by file-size tier; alert on `kafka.consumer.lag_seconds{lane=large} > 300` or `{lane=small} > 30`; track `worker.pool.utilization` per lane (alert >80% sustained); dashboard of worker-seconds demanded vs supplied per lane.

bottlenecks.title: DLQ accumulation from persistent OCR/ClamAV failures on malformed inputs
bottlenecks.trigger: Failure rate 0.5% at 10K commits/s = 50 fail/s, and after 3 retries (exponential backoff, ~10s total) ~5–10/s land in DLQ sustained — ~500K/day. Tika/Tesseract OCR crashes on malformed PDFs, exotic encodings, or oversized inputs; ClamAV updates can introduce regressions; a single bad signature update or adversarial file (zip bomb, malformed Office doc) can spike the failure rate 100× to thousands/s.
bottlenecks.symptom: DLQ size grows unboundedly; files stuck in status=READY but permanently without thumbnails/search; a worker pod OOMs on a zip-bomb PDF and restarts, losing in-flight state and re-processing from Kafka offset; 'search for my doc' returns nothing for some users; on-call drowns in low-sev DLQ alerts and starts ignoring them.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Sandbox each OCR/scan stage in a resource-bounded subprocess (cgroup memory cap 2GB, CPU timeout 60s, no network) so one bad file can't take down a worker; classify DLQ by failure type (timeout, OOM, parser-exception, AV-crash) and route to different remediation paths; auto-mark files as 'scan-failed' after DLQ and allow user-facing download to proceed (degrade gracefully — no thumbnail but file usable); size DLQ alerting on growth rate, not absolute count.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `worker.dlq.size` growth rate > 100/min (spike detection) rather than absolute threshold; track `worker.failure_rate` bucketed by failure-type and by mime_type (any mime exceeding 5% failure is suspect); monitor `worker.oom_kills` and `worker.subprocess_timeout_count` per pod (non-zero warrants investigation); per-stage success rate (fetch, thumbnail, AV, OCR, index) to localize which stage regresses after a deploy.

bottlenecks.title: Cloud storage block-fetch bandwidth bottleneck on file reassembly
bottlenecks.trigger: Every worker task must re-fetch all blocks of the committed file to run OCR/thumbnail/AV — a 1 GB file = 250 blocks × 4 MB downloaded from cloud storage per processing pass. At 10K commits/s averaging 1 MB = ~10 GB/s of egress into the worker fleet, and large-file processing amplifies this: 500 large files/s × 1 GB each = 500 GB/s theoretical peak egress from cloud storage into workers, well above steady-state upload bandwidth of 12 GB/s.
bottlenecks.symptom: Worker pod NIC pegged at 90%+ while CPU idle; S3 GET throttling (503 SlowDown) on hot block prefixes when many workers fetch the same recently-uploaded blocks; worker processing duration dominated by block-fetch time rather than actual work; cross-AZ egress bill spikes if workers aren't co-located with the cloud-storage bucket.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Co-locate worker pods in the same region/AZ as the cloud-storage bucket to avoid cross-AZ transfer costs and latency; cache recently-uploaded blocks locally on the worker pod for the processing window (LRU, ~50 GB ephemeral disk) since the same blocks were just PUT and are likely still in S3's hot cache; stream-process by block index rather than downloading full file first (thumbnail of page 1 doesn't need page 250); use byte-range GETs to skip irrelevant sections of large PDFs.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor `worker.nic.util_pct` per pod (alert >75% sustained 5 min); track `worker.block_fetch.duration_ms` as a fraction of total `worker.processing_duration_ms` (alert if >60% — indicates I/O-bound); `s3.get.throttled_count` from the worker fleet's IAM identity; per-pod `worker.cross_az_bytes_transferred` to catch co-location regressions.
