prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Upload Worker is here for Google Drive When a user hits save on a 50 MB presentation, the `/commit` call has to return in a few hundred milliseconds — the sync agent is blocking, the UI is spinning, and the user's other devices expect a notification within a second. But there's a pile of expensive work that *should* happen after every upload: generate thumbnails at multiple resolutions, run a malware scan (ClamAV), extract text for search (OCR on PDFs, parsing Office docs), and check whether old revisions should now tier down to cold storage. Doing any of that inline would turn a 300ms commit into a 10-second wait. The Upload Worker exists so the API can write the metadata row, drop one tiny event onto Kafka, and return — while a separate fleet chews through the expensive stuff asynchronously. ## What happens without it If the API did this synchronously, every upload would block on Tika and ClamAV. Users would watch "Saving…" spinners for 5–30 seconds on large files. Worse, if the thumbnail service had a bad deploy, *commits themselves* would start failing — one flaky downstream takes out the entire write path. Operators would see API concurrency (3,000 slots per replica) fill with threads parked on OCR, then unrelated endpoints like `/share` and `/download` start returning 503s. ## The number Peak write load is ~10K commits/sec, and processing takes 50–500ms per file (up to 30s for a 1 GB video). At 10,000/sec × 500ms = **5,000 worker-seconds of demand per real second** — you cannot do this inline without a 5,000× concurrency multiplier on the API tier. The queue absorbs bursts and lets ~200 worker pods drain at their own pace. ## Trade-off Thumbnails and search results become eventually-consistent (visible seconds-to-minutes after upload) in exchange for a fast, reliable commit path.

notify.name: Notification Service
notify.summary: Long-poll / WebSocket fan-out that keeps every signed-in device of a user (and every collaborator) in sync in near-real-time. This is the book's notification service — the thing that makes Drive feel instant across devices.

sections.heading: Multi-device sync (the book's headline use)
sections.body: Every signed-in client holds a long-poll HTTP connection on `/changes?since=rev`. When the API commits a new rev, it publishes to the notification service, which finds all that user's active connections (across their laptop, phone, tablet) AND all collaborators' connections, and pushes the delta. The client then re-syncs by fetching just the changed block hashes.

sections.heading: Channels
sections.body:
- Long-poll HTTP (simplest, works behind any proxy)
- WebSocket for active web sessions (lower overhead)
- APNs / FCM for mobile background push
- Email for @mentions and share events

sections.heading: Fan-out
sections.body: On a commit or share event: look up the set of (owner's devices ∪ collaborators' devices), then enqueue per-channel delivery jobs. Presence tracking tells us which devices are currently connected so offline ones fall back to mobile push.

sections.heading: Delivery semantics
sections.body: At-least-once; clients dedupe by `(file_id, rev)`. Order is best-effort per user (WebSocket is FIFO per connection; mobile push may re-order).

gained: Very simple, low-latency fan-out for WebSocket
lost: No persistence: a subscriber offline during publish misses the message — must be paired with a durable log

bottlenecks.title: 90M persistent connections overwhelm single-node socket capacity
bottlenecks.trigger: 100M DAU × 3 devices × 30% online = 90M concurrent long-poll/WebSocket connections. With a practical ceiling of ~500K connections per node (ephemeral ports, fd limits, kernel memory for TCP buffers at ~10KB/conn = 5GB RAM just for sockets), the fleet needs 180+ dedicated notification nodes just to hold sockets open — before any push traffic. A single deploy or AZ failure re-homing 30M connections creates a reconnect thundering herd.
bottlenecks.symptom: Connection refused / SYN drops during deploys; `nf_conntrack: table full` kernel messages; push latency jumps from ~1s to 30s+ during rebalances; on-call sees sawtooth pattern on `notify.active_connections` correlated with sync lag spikes; multi-device sync feels broken to users right after any infra change.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard connections by consistent hash(user_id) across 200+ nodes so fan-out lookups stay local; use SO_REUSEPORT with multiple accept queues; tune `net.core.somaxconn=65535`, `fs.file-max=10M`, and TCP memory autoscaling; prefer WebSocket over long-poll to cut reconnect rate 10x; implement graceful connection draining with 10-min bleed-off on deploys; fall back to FCM/APNs for mobile so they don't hold sockets in background.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-node `notify.active_connections` histogram (alert >400K = 80% of ceiling); `notify.reconnect_storm_rate` (reconnects/sec — alert >100K/sec fleet-wide); `kernel.nf_conntrack_count` vs `max` ratio (alert >70%); `notify.push_latency_p99_ms` SLO <2s with paging alert at 5s.

bottlenecks.title: Fan-out amplification on hot shared files and viral events
bottlenecks.trigger: Shared files (1% of 50B = 500M files, avg 3 collaborators) plus user's own 3 devices means every commit fans out to ~6 push targets on average, but hot collaborative files (large team drives, viral docs) can have hundreds of collaborators. At peak 10K commits/s with even 0.1% hitting high-fanout files with 200 collaborators, fan-out spikes from ~60K pushes/s steady to 200K+ pushes/s bursts — with presence lookups amplifying per-event work.
bottlenecks.symptom: Push latency tail grows from 1s to 30s for edits on team-shared docs; notification service CPU spikes correlated with commits on specific file_ids; `notify.fanout_queue_depth` climbs during business-hour bursts; collaborators complain 'I'm not seeing Alice's edits in real-time' while solo users are fine; presence-lookup Redis shard hotspots.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Batch per-recipient: coalesce multiple rev bumps on the same file within a 500ms window into one push; cap synchronous fan-out at 50 recipients and queue the rest to a background worker pool; use a presence cache keyed by user_id with pub/sub invalidation to avoid DB round-trips in the hot path; for mega-shared files (>100 collaborators), fall back to having clients poll /changes rather than push; rate-limit pushes per-recipient to prevent a rapid-save loop from flooding a single user.
bottlenecks.detection: Histogram `notify.fanout_size` per event (alert p99 > 50 recipients); track `notify.push_latency_ms` bucketed by fanout_size; per-file_id top-10 by push rate dashboard; `notify.fanout_queue_depth` sustained > 10K is a leading indicator of saturation.

bottlenecks.title: Presence/routing state consistency breaks during node failures
bottlenecks.trigger: Each user's 3 devices may be connected to different notification nodes (consistent hashing places user, but connections from multiple regions can land on different shards). Presence state (which device is on which node) must be queried on every fan-out. A node failure instantly invalidates ~500K presence entries, and the 2% failure rate in the sim means a 20-node fleet sees a node failure every few hours — each triggering a presence refresh storm and a reconnect wave.
bottlenecks.symptom: Events silently dropped for users whose device was on the failed node until they reconnect (delivery gap of 10–60s); duplicate pushes delivered to reconnected devices via multiple stale presence entries; `/changes?since=rev` catch-up traffic spikes 50x on node recovery; customer reports 'I missed an edit' after transient network issues.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use at-least-once delivery with durable outbox: persist fan-out intent to Kafka before attempting push, so a failed node's in-flight events are picked up by a peer; presence TTL of 30s with heartbeat every 10s so stale entries auto-expire; client-side dedupe by (file_id, rev) is already in design — enforce strictly; on reconnect, client sends last_seen_rev and server replays missed events from the change feed (bounded to last 24h); health-check ejection with 30s slow-start to avoid flooding recovered nodes.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `notify.delivery_gap_ms` p99 via client-side ack (push_sent_ts vs client_received_ts); alert on `notify.presence.stale_entries` > 1% of active; `notify.duplicate_pushes_suppressed` rate (rising indicates presence churn); SLO: 99.9% of commits result in a push to every online device within 5s, measured via sampled end-to-end probes.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Notification Service is here for Google Drive Drive isn't just "upload a file and forget about it" — it's a *sync* product. When you save a doc on your laptop, your phone and tablet are expected to show the new version within seconds, and any collaborator on a shared file expects the same. Without a dedicated push channel, every client would have to poll the API every few seconds asking "anything new?" — which at 100M DAU × 3 devices polling every 5s is **60M requests/sec** of wasted load, almost all returning "nothing changed." The Notification Service exists so the API can *tell* devices when something changed, instead of devices constantly asking. ## What happens without it If you ripped this out and replaced it with polling, users would see sync lag of 5–30 seconds depending on poll interval — edits on one device appearing minutes later on another. Operators would watch the API tier and metadata DB melt under poll traffic that's 99% no-op reads. Push the poll interval up to reduce load and users start complaining "Drive used to feel instant." The metadata cache hit rate stays high but the API concurrency budget fills with useless requests, starving real work like uploads and shares. ## The number The design estimates **90M active long-poll/WebSocket connections** (100M DAU × 3 devices × 30% online at once). At peak 10K commits/sec with avg ~6 fan-out targets (owner's 3 devices + 3 collaborators), that's ~60K pushes/sec — tractable when a dedicated service holds the sockets and does fan-out, impossible if every commit had to scan 90M connections on the API tier. ## Trade-off You accept operating a stateful, connection-heavy service (hard to deploy, hard to fail over) in exchange for sync feeling instant.

search.name: Search Indexer
search.summary: Elasticsearch cluster indexing filenames, full-text (OCR'd), and metadata for in-Drive search.

sections.heading: Index shape
sections.body:
```
index: files file_id keyword owner_id keyword # filter name text (autocomplete analyzer) content text (standard analyzer, truncated to 1 MB) mime keyword shared_with [keyword] # ACL for query-time filter updated_at date
```

sections.heading: Ingestion
sections.body: Worker emits `{file_id, owner_id, name, content,...}` after text extraction. Indexer bulk-writes every 5s (1K doc batches).

sections.heading: ACL filtering
sections.body: Every query is rewritten to `AND (owner_id:$u OR shared_with:$u)` — cheaper than post-filter, and it respects permissions at index-time.

sections.heading: Size
sections.body: 5B indexed files * ~2 KB indexed payload ≈ 10 TB. ES cluster with 20 data nodes, 2 replicas, RF-tuned for search latency.

bottlenecks.title: ACL fan-out explosion on share events bloats shared_with arrays
bottlenecks.trigger: Design has ~500M shared files (1% of 50B) with avg 3 collaborators, but team drives and company-wide shares can push shared_with arrays into thousands of principals. Every share event triggers a scripted _update on the doc (see share operation), and at peak share rates plus cascading folder-level share inheritance, a single parent-folder share can fan out to 10K+ child doc updates. ES array fields >1K entries degrade query performance and scripted updates rewrite the whole doc.
bottlenecks.symptom: Search query latency p99 climbs from ~50ms to 500ms+ for users in large orgs; shared_with arrays hit Lucene's practical field cardinality limits causing mapping explosion warnings; bulk share operations (share a folder with 500 people) take minutes to propagate to search; indexing queue backs up after org-wide share events.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Replace shared_with inline array with a separate `acl_index` document keyed by (principal, file_id) and use ES parent-child or terms-lookup query at search time (query-time join against a small per-user ACL doc). For folder-level shares, don't propagate to every child — resolve folder ancestry at query time via a folder_path field. Cap shared_with inline at 100 principals; beyond that, fall back to the terms-lookup path. Batch ACL updates via bulk API with 1K-doc batches.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `es.indexing.latency_p99_ms{op=update} > 200` or any doc where `shared_with.length > 500`. Track `es.query.latency_p99_ms` bucketed by user's org size (collaborators count). Monitor `es.bulk.queue_depth` after share events — sustained >10K indicates fan-out amplification.

bottlenecks.title: Indexing throughput can't keep up with commit rate on large-file OCR payloads
bottlenecks.trigger: Peak 10K commits/s × ~30% with extractable text (PDFs, Office docs) = ~3K indexing ops/s, each carrying up to 1 MB of OCR'd content. That's ~3 GB/s of indexing payload into a 20-node ES cluster = 150 MB/s per data node of pure index writes, before considering the 2 replicas (3x write amplification → 450 MB/s/node effective). Lucene segment merging on 10 TB indices with heavy updates triggers merge throttling.
bottlenecks.symptom: Bulk indexer lag grows from 5s to minutes during peak commit hours; `_bulk` returns 429 TOO_MANY_REQUESTS with queue_size exceeded; search results show files as missing for 5–30 min after upload; ES JVM heap pressure from segment merges causes GC pauses of 1–5s; indexing thread pool rejections in logs.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Truncate indexed content more aggressively (256 KB instead of 1 MB — 95% of search value comes from first pages); use `index.refresh_interval=30s` (up from default 1s) to batch segment creation; increase bulk batch from 1K to 5K docs with 10s flush window; separate hot indexing tier from cold search tier with ILM rollover (weekly indices); add 10 more data nodes sized for write throughput, not storage. Consider async replication (in-sync replicas=1) for the indexing path.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `es.bulk.rejected_count > 0` or `es.indexing.lag_seconds > 60`. Track `es.thread_pool.write.queue` (alert >80% of capacity), `es.jvm.gc.old.collection_time_ms > 500`, and `es.merges.current_docs` (sustained high indicates merge backpressure). SLI: 99% of commits searchable within 30s.

bottlenecks.title: Hot shard query concentration on power users' corpora
bottlenecks.trigger: Index is ~10 TB across 5B docs with ES's default routing by _id. Power users (enterprise tenants with millions of files) and any query filtered by `owner_id:$u` must fan out to all shards (no routing key match), causing every search to hit all 20 data nodes. At peak search QPS (estimated ~5K from read QPS mix), that's 100K shard-level queries/s across the cluster, and high-cardinality owner filtering doesn't prune shards.
bottlenecks.symptom: Search p99 latency 2–5x worse than p50 even on simple queries; ES search thread pool saturates during business hours; 'slow log' shows single-term queries taking 500ms+ because they fan out to 20 shards; top-heavy tenants (Acme Corp searching 10M of their own files) dominate cluster CPU; coordinator-node network saturates gathering results.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use custom routing: `index.routing.path=owner_id` so a user's docs live on a single shard — query-time `?routing=$owner_id` prunes from 20 shards to 1. For shared-with queries (can't route), use adaptive replica selection and a dedicated cross-tenant query pool. Split into per-tenant-size index tiers: small tenants in a shared index with routing, mega-tenants (>1M files) get dedicated indices. Cap request_cache to boost repeat filter performance.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `es.search.query_time_ms` p99 vs p50 ratio (alert >4x indicates fan-out overhead). Monitor `es.thread_pool.search.queue` and per-shard QPS variance (coefficient of variation >0.5 signals hotspots). Top-10 owner_id by query rate dashboard; alert if any owner >10% of cluster search CPU for 10 min.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Drive needs a dedicated search index Google Drive users expect to type "tax return 2022" and find the PDF within a few hundred milliseconds — across 50 billion files globally, filtered to just the ~10,000 files they personally own or have access to. The Metadata DB can't do this. It's sharded by `owner_id` and indexed for lookups like "list the contents of folder X" or "get file by id." It has no full-text index on filenames, and it certainly doesn't store the OCR'd contents of PDFs or the text extracted from Office docs. Asking MySQL to `WHERE name LIKE '%tax%'` across a 100-shard cluster would scan billions of rows and melt the database. The Search Indexer (Elasticsearch) exists because *search is a fundamentally different access pattern* from "fetch this file by id" — it needs inverted indexes, relevance scoring, and autocomplete analyzers that a relational store doesn't provide. ## What happens without it Remove ES and the search box either disappears or routes to the Metadata DB. Users see "Search timed out" errors or 10+ second waits. The operator watches MySQL CPU pin to 100% on every search, read replicas fall behind, and *unrelated* operations like file listings and permission checks start timing out. Drive essentially becomes unusable for any user with more than a few hundred files, because finding anything requires remembering exactly which folder it's in. ## The number The design indexes **~5B files × ~2 KB payload ≈ 10 TB** of searchable content. At estimated ~5K search QPS (a fraction of the 25K peak reads), each query must filter by ACL (`owner_id:$u OR shared_with:$u`) and return results in <100ms — only possible with pre-built inverted indexes on 20 ES data nodes, each holding ~500 GB. ## Trade-off Search results lag uploads by seconds-to-minutes (eventual consistency via the Upload Queue) in exchange for sub-100ms queries at massive scale.

operations.title: Upload a file (delta sync + block-level dedup)
operations.name: Upload a file (delta sync + block-level dedup)
operations.description: Client splits a 12 MB file into three 4 MB blocks. Two blocks already exist globally (dedup hit) OR exist in a prior revision (delta sync hit), one is new. Only the new block is uploaded via the block server. Other devices are notified within ~1s.

steps.title: User drops report.pdf (12 MB) into Drive
steps.action: Desktop agent splits the file into three 4 MB blocks and computes SHA-256 for each. It does NOT upload yet — first it negotiates with the API.
steps.codeOrCommand:
blocks = split_fixed(file, 4 * 1024 * 1024)
# blocks = [b0, b1, b2] each 4 MB
hashes = [sha256(b).hex for b in blocks]
# hashes = [
# "a1b2c3...e5", # b0 — appeared in a shared template before (dedup hit)
# "f4d8e2...90", # b1 — identical to previous revision (delta sync hit)
# "9c7e1a...42", # b2 — genuinely new bytes
# ]
steps.note: Computing 3 SHA-256's on 12 MB takes ~40ms on a modern laptop — negligible vs the network upload.

steps.title: LB routes to an API replica
steps.action: L7 round-robin; POST /files is not sticky. Any API replica can accept the upload initiation.
steps.codeOrCommand:
upstream = pool.pick(algo="round_robin", healthy_only=True)
forward(req -> upstream)

steps.title: API (metadata service) creates file row status=UPLOADING
steps.action: API authenticates the user, checks quota, and inserts a pending file row with status UPLOADING and rev=1. Blocks are NOT written yet — the manifest is tentative until `/commit`. API forwards the hash list to the block servers for dedup resolution.
steps.codeOrCommand:
user = auth.verify(req.bearer)
if quota.used(user) + req.size > quota.cap(user): return 413 file_id = idgen.next
db.execute(""" INSERT INTO files (id, owner_id, parent_id, name, size_bytes, rev, status) VALUES (?,?,?,?,?, 1, 'UPLOADING')
""", (file_id, user.id, req.parent_id, req.name, req.size))

steps.title: Block server resolves dedup + delta sync
steps.action: For each hash, the block server first hits the Redis Bloom filter. Filter hits are verified against the authoritative cloud-storage index (S3 HEAD). Existing blocks get action=skip; new blocks get a pre-signed PUT URL scoped to that block's hash key. This is where both cross-user dedup AND intra-user delta sync are enforced.
steps.codeOrCommand: results = for h in req.hashes: if not redis.bf_exists("block_bf", h): url = cloud_storage.presigned_put(key=block_key(h), ttl=900) results.append({"hash": h, "action": "upload", "url": url}) else: if cloud_storage.head(block_key(h)): results.append({"hash": h, "action": "skip"}) else: url = cloud_storage.presigned_put(key=block_key(h), ttl=900) results.append({"hash": h, "action": "upload", "url": url})

steps.title: API returns upload plan to client
steps.action: The response tells the client exactly which blocks to upload (1 of 3) and where. Two blocks are deduped away — we just saved 8 MB of upload bandwidth.
steps.codeOrCommand:
return Response(201, { "file_id": 7721893, "rev": 1, "plan": [ {"idx": 0, "hash": "a1b2c3...e5", "action": "skip"}, {"idx": 1, "hash": "f4d8e2...90", "action": "skip"}, {"idx": 2, "hash": "9c7e1a...42", "action": "upload", "url": "https://s3.../9c7e1a...42?X-Amz-Signature=..."} ]
})
steps.decision: 2/3 blocks are dedup/delta hits — client skips upload for them

steps.title: Client sends only the missing block through block server
steps.action: The block server compresses + encrypts the block (in some deployments the client does this client-side first) and stores it in cloud storage via the presigned URL. The API and LB are out of the data path for the bytes themselves.

steps.title: Cloud storage accepts and durably stores the block
steps.action: Writes the object, computes its own checksum, and replicates across AZs (erasure-coded 10+4). Returns 200 with an ETag matching the SHA-256 we supplied.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# conceptual
placement = CRUSH.pick("blocks/9c/7e/9c7e1a...42")
write_erasure_coded(placement, body)
# durability: 11 9's, cross-AZ

steps.title: Client calls /commit to finalize
steps.action: After the one block lands, client calls PUT /files/:id/commit. This is the transaction that flips status from UPLOADING to READY and bumps rev.
steps.codeOrCommand: http.put(f"/files/{file_id}/commit", json={"rev": 1})

steps.title: API writes block manifest + version row, flips status to READY
steps.action: Single-shard transaction: insert 3 rows into `blocks` (rev=2), append a `versions` row, flip `files.status` to READY, bump `files.rev`. Any unexpectedly missing block fails commit with 409.

steps.title: API enqueues a post-upload event (parallel)
steps.action: Fire-and-forget produce to Kafka so the worker picks up thumbnail / OCR / indexing / version-retention sweep.
steps.codeOrCommand:
producer.send("file-committed", key=str(user.id), value={ "file_id": 7721893, "owner_id": user.id, "rev": 2, "mime": "application/pdf", "size_bytes": 12582912, "ts": now_epoch
})

steps.title: API warms Redis with the new file row (parallel)
steps.action: Write-through cache so the next GET /files/7721893 is a Redis hit; teach the block Bloom filter about the new hash.
steps.codeOrCommand:
redis.setex(f"file:7721893", 300, json.dumps(file_row))
redis.bf_add("block_bf", "9c7e1a...42")

steps.title: Notification service pushes delta to user's other devices
steps.action: The API calls the notification service with the new rev. The service looks up the user's active long-poll / WebSocket connections (phone, tablet, laptop-2) AND any collaborators, and pushes `{file_id, rev, changed_blocks: [2]}`. Those devices will immediately fetch the single new block and reassemble.
steps.codeOrCommand:
connections = presence.connections_for(user_id=12) + collaborators_of(7721893)
for ch in connections: ch.push({"type": "file-updated", "file_id": 7721893, "rev": 2, "changed_blocks": [2]})

steps.title: API returns 200 to the uploading client
steps.action: Commit OK; user sees the file show up in their Drive UI. Total wall-clock: ~300ms (mostly the 4 MB block upload).

steps.title: LB relays 200 back
steps.action: Return path.

steps.title: Desktop agent shows the file as synced
steps.action: UI flips from 'uploading' to 'synced'. Because 2/3 blocks were deduped (one cross-user, one intra-user delta), effective upload was 4 MB not 12 MB — on a 10 Mbps link that's 3.2s instead of 9.6s. Other devices light up within ~1s.

operations.title: Download a file
operations.name: Download a file
operations.description: User opens a 12 MB PDF. API returns the manifest, client pulls 3 blocks in parallel directly from cloud storage (via the block server's signed URLs) and reassembles.

steps.title: User clicks report.pdf
steps.action: Client requests the file metadata + block manifest with signed download URLs.
steps.codeOrCommand: http.get(f"/files/7721893/download")

steps.title: LB forwards to an API replica
steps.action: Standard L7 routing.

steps.title: API checks Redis for the file row
steps.action: Before touching SQL, look up `file:7721893` in Redis.
steps.codeOrCommand:
row = redis.get(f"file:7721893")
if row is None: row = db.fetchone("SELECT * FROM files WHERE id = 7721893") redis.setex(f"file:7721893", 300, json.dumps(row))

steps.title: Redis returns the file row (HIT)
steps.action: File row was cached by the upload path; still within 5 min TTL. O(1) memory lookup.
steps.decision: Cache HIT — skip SQL fetch for file row

steps.title: API loads the block manifest (3 rows for rev=2)
steps.action: Blocks are not cached in Redis (too many, rarely re-read). Single-shard indexed read.
steps.codeOrCommand:
SELECT idx, hash, size
FROM blocks
WHERE file_id = 7721893 AND rev = 2
ORDER BY idx ASC;

steps.title: Block server issues 3 signed GET URLs
steps.action: API asks the block-server tier to issue presigned GET URLs for each hash. If any block has aged into cold storage, the block server transparently initiates a re-hydration.
steps.codeOrCommand:
urls = [{ "idx": b.idx, "url": cloud_storage.presigned_get(block_key(b.hash), ttl=300)
} for b in blocks]

steps.title: API returns manifest + URLs
steps.action: One response carries everything the client needs to assemble the file.

steps.title: LB relays 200
steps.action: Return path.

steps.title: Client fetches 3 blocks in parallel
steps.action: Desktop agent opens 3 parallel HTTP GETs to cloud storage. With ~40 MB/s per connection, total wall-clock is ~300ms (parallel, not 900ms sequential).
steps.codeOrCommand:
async def fetch_all: return await asyncio.gather( http.get(plan.blocks[0].url), http.get(plan.blocks[1].url), http.get(plan.blocks[2].url), )
bytes_ = await fetch_all

steps.title: Cloud storage streams each block back
steps.action: 3 parallel reads; each is ~10–40ms first byte + streaming throughput. Blocks are immutable so this is a pure read — no lock contention.

steps.title: Client decrypts, decompresses, reassembles in order
steps.action: Concatenate in idx order and hand the bytes to the PDF viewer. Total perceived download: ~400–600ms on a decent connection.
steps.codeOrCommand:
file_bytes = b"".join(decompress(decrypt(bytes_[i])) for i in sorted_by_idx)
# hand to OS / renderer

operations.title: Multi-device sync via notification service
operations.name: Multi-device sync via notification service
operations.description: User edits report.pdf on their laptop. Their phone + tablet (same account) are signed in with long-poll connections held open by the notification service. Within ~1s of commit, both pick up the new rev and fetch just the changed block.

steps.title: Laptop commits edit (rev 3)
steps.action: Same upload flow as before but only the changed 4 MB block is new.

steps.title: API writes rev 3, notifies
steps.action: Single-shard commit. API then publishes the rev-bump to the notification service.

steps.title: Notify service fans out to same-user devices
steps.action: Looks up presence: phone (long-poll open), tablet (WebSocket open), another laptop (offline → mobile push). Delivers a `{file_id, rev: 3, changed_blocks: [i]}` event to each.

steps.title: Phone + tablet receive push
steps.action: Each device's agent reacts by calling GET /files/7721893 to get the new manifest, then fetches only the one changed block — delta sync end-to-end.

steps.title: Devices now show the new version
steps.action: Total latency commit→all devices updated ≈ 1–2s.

operations.title: Share a file with a collaborator
operations.name: Share a file with a collaborator
operations.description: User shares report.pdf with alice@. API updates the ACL, notifies Alice via the notification service (WebSocket + mobile push + email), and re-indexes the file for her search scope.

steps.title: User picks 'Share with alice@'
steps.action: UI sends POST /files/:id/share with the target principal and role.
steps.codeOrCommand:
http.post(f"/files/7721893/share", json={ "principal": "alice@example.com", "role": "EDITOR"
})

steps.title: LB forwards to an API replica
steps.action: Standard L7 routing.

steps.title: API verifies owner permission
steps.action: Look up the requesting user's role on the file. Must be OWNER or EDITOR with share rights.

steps.title: API writes the new ACL row and bumps file rev
steps.action: Single-shard transaction. Bumping rev signals the change-feed that something changed about this file.

steps.title: Invalidate cached ACL entries (parallel)
steps.action: Permissions changed — drop the stale `acl:alice:7721893` key and the file row so the next read re-fetches fresh.
steps.codeOrCommand:
redis.delete("acl:887654:7721893")
redis.delete("file:7721893")
redis.publish("invalidations", "file:7721893")

steps.title: Notification service fans out to Alice
steps.action: Look up Alice's active channels (WebSocket, mobile devices, email pref). Enqueue one push per channel. Email is throttled to hourly digest if Alice has that pref.
steps.codeOrCommand:
channels = presence.channels_for(user_id=887654)
for ch in channels: if ch.kind == "ws": ws.send(ch, json.dumps({"type": "shared", "file_id": 7721893})) elif ch.kind == "fcm": fcm.send(ch.token, title="User shared report.pdf", data={"file_id": "7721893"}) elif ch.kind == "email": email.enqueue(to="alice@example.com", template="share", ctx={...})

steps.title: Re-index the file for Alice's search scope (parallel)
steps.action: Update the file's `shared_with` array so search queries from Alice now match this file. Single ES update by doc id.

steps.title: API returns 200 to the sharer
steps.action: Commit succeeded; Alice will receive the notification within seconds.

steps.title: LB relays 200
steps.action: Return path.

steps.title: Sharer UI shows 'Shared with Alice'
steps.action: Alice's devices light up with a push notification within ~2s; her desktop sync picks it up on its next /changes long-poll (within ~5s).

operations.title: Version retention → cold storage migration
operations.name: Version retention → cold storage migration
operations.description: Background sweep: after a file accumulates more than N versions OR blocks age out of the active retention window, the orphaned blocks move from hot cloud storage to cold storage, reclaiming space without losing the ability to view old versions.

steps.title: Periodic retention sweep event
steps.action: A scheduled producer enqueues sweep tasks per shard.

steps.title: Worker scans expiring versions
steps.action: For each file with > N versions, find versions beyond the retention window and decrement refcounts on their exclusive blocks.

steps.title: Mark blocks as tier=cold in manifest
steps.action: Update metadata so downloads of old versions know to expect higher latency / fetch via cold-tier path.

steps.title: Copy block to cold storage, delete from hot
steps.action: Move operation: write to cold, verify, then delete from hot. Keeps the durability invariant at all times.

steps.title: Block lands in cold / offline-backup tier
steps.action: Stored at ~4x lower $/GB. Available for retrieval in ms (Instant Retrieval) or minutes (Standard) depending on tier choice.

tradeoffs.rationale: Simple to reason about, cheap to index, and good enough dedup for typical office files. Content-defined chunking would dedup better for appended logs but complicates the client.

tradeoffs.chosen: Sharded SQL sharded by user_id with a Redis cache
tradeoffs.rationale: A user's edits need serializable ordering for revisions; SQL gives that trivially. Sharding by user_id keeps cross-shard transactions out of the hot path. Redis absorbs hot-file reads.

tradeoffs.chosen: Long-poll or WebSocket notification service with pull-based delta fetch
tradeoffs.rationale: Push only a tiny 'something changed' signal; let the client pull with its last-known revision. Keeps the push fabric stateless and handles reconnects correctly.

tradeoffs.chosen: Last N revisions or time-based, older tiered to cold storage
tradeoffs.rationale: A user rewriting the same doc 100 times would otherwise 100x the storage for that file. Trades instant restore latency for older versions for huge cost savings.
Same viral PDF shared by a million users is stored once. Requires per-block refcounting and careful GC; gains ~30% storage overall.
